title: Medicine Needs to Get Serious About AI
excerpt: For as long as ChatGPT has existed, Americans have been asking it, “Could that funny little spot on my toe be cancer?” And as AI has advanced over the past few
body: For as long as ChatGPT has existed, Americans have been asking it, “Could that funny little spot on my toe be cancer?” And as AI has advanced over the past few years, doctors have begun to use specialized models to ask much the same questions in clinics
In the face of these developments, professional medical societies have presented a unified front: Doctors must always have the final say in clinical care

As the medical societies allow, physicians’ enhancing their work with AI tools may be a perfectly good way to deliver medicine. (One of us—Khosla—has in fact invested in a primary-care start-up, co-founded by his son, in which doctors supervise AI assistants.) But for Americans to get the best health care possible, we need to be willing to experiment with models that put AI in control
This notion has caused a stir in the medical community

When we published a commentary in the Journal of the American Medical Association last month arguing that AI-only care could soon become superior to care provided by human physicians, the CEO of the American Medical Association denounced us as undermining the patient-doctor relationship
The organization’s position was unchanged: AI should be relegated to a supporting role in clinical care
It’s an argument that ignores the available evidence and could hold untold numbers of Americans back from better health
Much of modern medicine—including managing hypertension, determining the right treatment for many cancers, and addressing chemotherapy side effects—is largely algorithmic

A physician needs to ask a patient targeted questions, determine possible diagnoses, order tests to identify the correct one, offer a treatment plan, and adjust it depending on how the patient responds
That series of actions is steered by detailed guidelines from professional societies
Yet doctors—despite the best of intentions—make plenty of mistakes when following those steps
Studies indicate that up to 15 percent of American patients are misdiagnosed each year, leading to tens of thousands of preventable deaths
That’s why health-care providers have software that notifies them if they, say, prescribe a deadly dose of a drug

Any software that could practice medicine autonomously would be similarly specialized: not generic ChatGPT, but a model trained in medical knowledge with the appropriate guardrails to minimize risks and mistakes
Such a model could check for drug interactions more consistently and comprehensively than physicians
And it would be able to check in with patients much more frequently than human health-care providers do
Some AI models have already proved adept at such tasks

In one study published last year, expert physicians judged Google’s Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer—a highly trained AI model for medical diagnosis and reasoning—as significantly better than human doctors at getting actors playing patients to open up
The “patients” revealed more about their complaints, along with their medical, family, and medication history, all of which can be crucial for an accurate diagnosis
In a 2023 study , patients with type 2 diabetes were randomized to have their insulin dose adjusted by physicians or autonomous AI
The machines got patients to a stable dose faster than human physicians, and their patients took their insulin more reliably and had less distress related to their diabetes
What about the physician-AI hybrids that medical associations are backing? Research on them is sparse, and more is needed

A 2025 review of 52 studies concluded that, on balance, such hybrids “neither outperformed medical AI alone nor surpassed the best of clinicians.” In at least a few of those studies, human-AI hybrids outperformed AI alone
But in those hybrid teams, the AI controlled the final clinical decision—the opposite of what the AMA and others have in mind
Medical organizations are not entirely closed-minded to the possibility of change

For example, last week the American College of Physicians published a position paper that allowed that “fully autonomous AI is possible,” but cautioned that its use should be infrequent and “limited to low-risk, low-complexity decisions, and always allow for bringing a clinician into the loop.” John Whyte, the CEO of the AMA, told The Atlantic that he was “disappointed” in the quality of the analysis in our JAMA commentary last month

He questioned the design of the studies we reviewed, many of which involved simulated situations with actors or a retrospective review of existing cases rather than real clinical outcomes, and did not follow patients for years or decades
We agree that longer-term, real-world studies are necessary; hopefully, once advanced AI medical tools have existed for more than a handful of years, results will begin to arrive

Whyte was enthusiastic about further study of physicians controlling AI tools, but only cautiously open to further exploration of autonomous AI in medicine, arguing that the latter would need to be highly regulated
Reasons exist, of course, to be skeptical of AI-driven medical care
In nine of the 51 studies we reviewed, human physicians outperformed the machines
But some of these tested older AI models or general-use AI models that weren’t trained on medical information and specific guardrails for patient care
Prominent physicians have also argued that real-life doctors are harried by 15-minute appointments and administrative burdens such as prior authorization
That is certainly true, but it is also irrelevant to many of the experiments we reviewed, which examined relatively hassle-free simulations of medical appointments
One of the most common objections to an AI-doctor future is that robots lack the human connection that patients need to build trust
The American College of Physicians’ recent position paper, for example, cited AI’s inability to make eye contact
But consider that doctors, too, can be robotic
In a Gallup survey conducted late last year, 21 percent of respondents said they had turned to AI because they had previously felt dismissed by a health-care provider
In the 2025 study of Google’s AMIE, patient actors reported that the AI was more emotionally supportive than the physicians were
In a systematic review of 15 studies comparing AI chatbots with physicians, 13 found that AI had significantly higher perceived empathy

title: Cereal Has Strayed Too Far
excerpt: Breakfast-cereal boxes are a window into both the politics of food and American culture
body: Breakfast-cereal boxes are a window into both the politics of food and American culture
As a particularly timely example, since Robert F
Kennedy Jr. took office last year as secretary of health and human services, he has called for the removal of artificial dyes from breakfast cereals

On Fox News in 2024, he lamented that the bright colors in Froot Loops are “literally poisoning our kids.” (How exactly these dyes interact with human health is complicated .) Cereal companies responded right away
General Mills announced last month that it had transitioned its entire U.S. portfolio of cereals—including Trix and Lucky Charms—to all-natural dyes made from fruits, veggies, and spices
Kellogg had previously announced plans to do the same by the end of 2027
Target stopped selling any cereals with artificial colors earlier this year
For the Make America Healthy Again movement, the removal of artificial dyes is a big win
But cereal still comes with a major concern for many consumers
Nearly all ready-to-eat breakfast cereals sold in the United States—and especially those marketed to children—are presweetened
The initial loading of breakfast cereals with sugar has been attributed to a single person: Jim Rex, a heating-equipment salesman who lived in Pennsylvania in the early 20th century
As the story goes, Rex was appalled by the spoonfuls of sugar his kids added to their breakfast cereals and set out to create a version that would not induce such behavior
His brilliant contribution: a glossy honey coating on puffed wheat, a cereal he named Ranger Joe Wheat Honnies in 1939
It didn’t take long for Rex’s strategy to backfire
Kellogg introduced Sugar Pops in 1951, Sugar Frosted Flakes in 1952, and Froot Loops in 1963, each among the company’s all-time best sellers
General Mills launched Sugar Smiles in 1953
The next year, the company added sugar and artificial colors to its Kix cereal, thus creating Trix
In 1950, such presweetened cereals represented just 5 percent of all cereals sold, but by the mid-1970s, kids accounted for almost 40 percent of all cereal consumption
In 2014, the Environmental Working Group estimated that kids could ingest about nine pounds of sugar a year just by eating a serving of cereal every day
Advocates for children’s health have long complained about the high sugar content of breakfast cereals
In the early 1970s, Congress held hearings to highlight cereal’s inadequate nutritional quality
Cereal companies objected, arguing, correctly, that grains are nutritious
But they also responded by trying to make their products appear less sugary
They began by removing the S-word from cereal names, and some substituted honey for sugar on the theory that people perceive honey as more wholesome and nutritious
In the 1990s, companies hit on another clever strategy: If they used multiple sugar types, they could list grains first on a product’s ingredients but sprinkle sugars throughout the list
Cereals looked healthier, but when Consumer Reports compared the sugars in 27 breakfast cereals in 2008, it found that many were still 50 percent sugar by weight

Rumors circulated that federal agencies were working to set nutrition standards for foods advertised on television programs aimed at children younger than 12, which would likely spell trouble for sugary cereals
In 2009, General Mills pledged to reduce sugar in its most popular kids’ cereals—most of which had at least 12 grams a serving—to single digits
Its pledge would apply to 10 cereals, including some of its most popular, such as Lucky Charms and Cocoa Puffs
By 2012, General Mills had reached the single-digit goal for Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Cookie Crisp, and more
Some of this success was due to decreased serving size
And the best General Mills could do for Lucky Charms was 10 grams of sugar in a three-quarters-cup serving—which the company found to be the minimum sweet spot for kids’ acceptance
The project had encountered a harsh reality: Kids like sugar, and companies remove it at their peril
Sugary cereal is not just a consumer concern; it is also a matter of government nutrition policy

Since 1980, the federal Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) has limited the sugars in cereals it will cover to six grams an ounce, about half of the amount in typical cereals aimed at kids
WIC can be a lucrative business for cereals that qualify, so the limit has induced companies to take two actions
The first is to formulate new cereals with less sugar specifically for the WIC market

In 2006, for example, General Mills introduced a new kid-targeted cereal, Dora the Explorer, “lightly sweetened cinnamon corn puffs,” with six grams of sugar in a 27-gram serving—an amount that meets the WIC standards
The second is to petition to change how sugar in cereals is counted
When the six-gram rule went into effect, in the early 1980s, Kellogg immediately objected

title: When Mothers Get Arrested for Mothering
excerpt: This past June, a Virginia mother named Karyann Parkinson took a bike ride with her 5-year-old son and stopped by a pond inside their gated community to collect
body: This past June, a Virginia mother named Karyann Parkinson took a bike ride with her 5-year-old son and stopped by a pond inside their gated community to collect goose feathers from the grass
The two of them rode back home, whereupon Parkinson’s son asked his mother if he could walk back to the pond by himself to fetch a few more feathers
Parkinson, who was eight months pregnant with her fifth child, studying for the bar exam, and—perhaps most pressing—making lunch, agreed

The walk was relatively short, along a sidewalk 10 feet from the road and across two intersections with crosswalks, which Parkinson knew her son could navigate successfully (he had done so six times that morning)
But on his way, the boy was spotted by a concerned passerby, who notified a community security guard, who in turn notified the police
Before long, several police officers were at Parkinson’s door, followed by Child Protective Services agents

Officials in the case decided to press charges against Parkinson, and last week she was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and placed on Virginia’s child-abuse-and-neglect registry, where she will remain for seven years

Parkinson told me that her son—who competently walked the security guard back to their house after politely explaining that he wasn’t allowed to get into cars with strangers—had become distraught upon learning that he had apparently done something very bad

And although the police treated Parkinson as though she were negligent, her husband, who works as a marriage and family therapist and sees a lot of anxious young adults, tried to explain to the officers that they had made a deliberate choice to let their children encounter appropriate levels of challenge and risk
Two weeks later, two police officers showed up at Parkinson’s door with a warrant for her arrest. “It just kept escalating,” she told me. “No one was taking a step back and going, Oh, this is fine
This is a fine situation .” She gave birth to her baby a week later
Last week’s guilty verdict, Parkinson said, has been disorienting

Having spent 15 years taking some pride in her mindful choices as a parent, she has lately been doubting herself—“and thinking, Am I really crazy? ” Her lawyers have appealed the decision, and Parkinson will receive a new trial

People are having fewer children around the world for a variety of reasons, but some observers suggest that the steep expectations placed on parents—and mothers in particular—may be at least partly to blame for the fertility cliff in the United States

In response to a pervasive atmosphere of parental stress, a number of social-media influencers and public intellectuals have recommended that parents just do less—no more assiduously planned birthday extravaganzas, no more enrichment programs scheduled from breakfast to bedtime, no more hawkish monitoring to rescue children from any hint of danger or discomfort. [ Derek Thompson: The great depopulation ] But even though working parents may long for the days when children were more independent—a wish reinforced by countless editorials declaring the wisdom of letting children roam freely, away from their screens—society seems to have irrevocably changed

Most families now include two parents working full-time , and although many of these adults enjoyed the unchaperoned pleasures of a latchkey existence, the sight of children left to their own devices now horrifies not only the neighbors but also cops and prosecutors
In other words, parents are caught in a vise made up of financial demands and socially inflated expectations around parenting

In 2008, Lenore Skenazy made national news when she published a column about letting her 9-year-old son ride the subway home after a trip to Bloomingdale’s in Midtown Manhattan, a decision that many people likewise characterized as a form of child abuse or neglect

Skenazy, who has since founded what she calls the Free-Range Kids movement, occasionally publishes stories about mothers who are arrested or locked up for letting their children enjoy what used to be considered ordinary childhood pleasures

In 2020, a Georgia mother of five was jailed for allowing her 14-year-old daughter to babysit her younger siblings during the pandemic, when schools and day-care facilities were closed but parents still had to work

In 2024, a mother of four in Georgia was handcuffed when her 10-year-old son was found walking into town, less than a mile from their home, while she was taking one of her other children to a doctor’s appointment

Parkinson’s story has become a national phenomenon in large part because Skenazy first called attention to it in Reason magazine. [ Read: The new parent trap ] Raising children comes with enough trade-offs without enforcing unforgiving standards for parental attention, entertainment, and supervision
Notably, none of the cases in which police arrested mothers for their presumed negligence involved children who had been actually harmed

One hesitates to admit to such a taboo practice in print, but my own 10-year-old daughter has ventured out unaccompanied to hang out with her friends or pick up a few things from the store, and although I have fretted over getting pinched by the police, she treasures those opportunities to establish some independence even more than I appreciate time away from monitoring and enabling her various whims and desires

Mixing in activities that don’t require constant parental oversight is unfortunately a daring practice these days, but it seems crucial to balancing work and other adult responsibilities with the demands of raising children
This is not to say that allowing kids some independence comes without risks: Cars pose a threat, as does every child’s latent desire to engage in mischief
Unknown adults assailing children with ill intentions, though a terrifying prospect, is exceedingly rare; stranger abductions account for less than 1 percent of missing-child cases nationwide

But these risks may nevertheless be overstated in our social imagination because ours is a low-trust society; in other countries , young people are granted much more freedom because parents presume that the adults they encounter will be helpful and supportive
What Parkinson, Skenazy, and many other parents understand is that independence is good for children , who stand to build confidence and competence by doing things on their own
And fostering that independence is, in the end, the primary goal of parenting
The job is hard and bittersweet by design: Every step they take in the world is a step away from you
This, of course, is where their journeys are destined to lead.

title: Why Lonnie Bunch Is Leaving the Smithsonian
excerpt: This story was updated at 4:12 p.m. on September 8, 2026
body: This story was updated at 4:12 p.m. on September 8, 2026

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch plans to retire from the institution at the end of this year, bringing to a close a tenure marked by unprecedented pressure on the museum complex from a White House keen on controlling how to tell the nation’s history

After a person with knowledge of the situation confirmed the departure to The Atlantic , Bunch addressed Smithsonian employees at a town hall this afternoon, telling them, “I may be going away, but I’m still going to be a pain in the ass to some people.” The crowd of staffers, who spilled out of an auditorium and into an overflow room at the Hirshhorn Museum, clapped and cheered, even as some likely wondered: Why now ? In conversations with intimates, Bunch has been floating his retirement since at least the beginning of this year
But the increased attention from the White House surely made stepping down an even more delicate decision

Bunch, who is 73, tried to deflect any notion that his departure was Trump-related, telling staffers, “I now realize that I’m old as dirt, and it’s time for the next chapter in my life.” He also suggested that the timing may have been influenced by his wife, Maria Marable-Bunch, who recently retired from the National Museum of the American Indian. “The Smithsonian represents more than a career to me; it’s been an integral part of who I am,” he said. “I think about during the many years here, I met the love of my life, who’s retired and told me I better retire soon.” Bunch’s exit will leave the Smithsonian, which is largely federally funded, with a vacancy at the top as it faces escalating efforts from the Trump administration to influence its work

Bunch, known to be diplomatic and evenhanded, had largely staved off the White House’s encroachment over a tumultuous 18 months in which the administration issued executive orders and letters criticizing the museums and threatened to withhold funding

In July, President Trump signed an executive order calling for signage to be added to the exterior of the National Museum of American History warning about what the administration claims is an inaccurate and partisan telling of history
Smithsonian leaders have countered that telling the American story fairly and accurately means discussing its complexities too
In a news release, Bunch said: “There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together

I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” The chair of the Smithsonian Board of Regents, Franklin D

Raines, thanked Bunch for his service and said the institution’s governing body will be “focused on ensuring stability during this time of transition.” He said that the Smithsonian would soon announce an acting secretary and begin a search for Bunch’s successor. “There are some very strong internal candidates,” Kim Sajet, the former director of the National Portrait Gallery, told us today

Before becoming secretary of the entire Smithsonian, Bunch was the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which has been widely praised for its powerful handling of the darkest chapters of America’s past
In Bunch, the Smithsonian had at its helm an advocate for its continued independence
The first historian and the first Black leader of the 21-museum complex, he spent nearly 38 years in roles across the institution

His departure has increased anxieties about the institution’s future. [ Read: First the Kennedy Center, now the Smithsonian ] “As the only Secretary of the Smithsonian to come from a background in history, he was well positioned to understand—and to defend—the discipline when history itself is under attack,” a former colleague of Bunch’s, who worked with him for years, texted us after the news. “His eloquent defense of history, grounded in a deeply rooted cultural understanding of the American story, will leave a leadership vacuum and the Smithsonian will be ever more vulnerable,” the colleague, who requested anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the administration, went on
In a way, Trump and Bunch exemplified a primary tension facing not only the Smithsonian in this moment but the field of American history more generally

Trump’s call for a feel-good, Founding Fathers–forward telling of American history is somewhat at odds with Bunch’s biggest achievements: the dramatic reevaluation of whose story has a place on the National Mall and how the country faces the harder parts of its past
Bunch will leave the institution just as it seeks to hold off a threat against the very work that defines his legacy
One of the most dramatic illustrations of that tension occurred in May 2025, when Trump announced that he was firing Sajet, even though he had no authority to do so

The Board of Regents affirmed Bunch’s authority over hiring and firing, though Sajet ultimately resigned from the National Portrait Gallery in June, saying that the dispute had become a distraction for the institution

Sajet, who now leads the Milwaukee Art Museum, told us she still misses the Smithsonian and has watched with dismay as the pressure that came for her first continues to bear down on her former colleagues
Through the changes, Sajet said that she and Bunch have remained in close touch. “I think it’s one of the loneliest jobs in the world to be in the head of a large institution like that,” she said

Sajet said Bunch’s background as both a historian and a museum director made him well suited to steer the Smithsonian through periods of turmoil—including the racial-justice reckoning after George Floyd’s murder and the pandemic. “I know that you believe that your legacy is building the National Museum of African American History and Culture,” Sajet recalled telling him. “But I’d like to suggest to you that you being the secretary at this particular moment in time is really important.” She said she believes those same qualities carried him through the Smithsonian’s showdowns with the White House, adding that he’s labored to maintain the institution’s unusual relationship with the federal government (all three branches are represented on the Board of Regents). “He’s tried very hard to maintain the respect for our elected officials, and I admire him for it,” Sajet said
Trump’s attacks at times seemed to directly target Bunch’s work

Last summer, the president came after the Smithsonian on social media, writing that it focused too much on “how bad Slavery was.” The two later met over lunch at the White House, a conversation that Bunch described as “the most stressful lunch I’ve ever had in my life.” In a December letter that the administration sent to the Smithsonian, the White House threatened to withhold funding if the museum complex did not comply with an order to send over a trove of documents about its work and comply with its demands to tell an adequately patriotic version of American history
Americans “will have no patience for any museum that is diffident about America’s founding or otherwise uncomfortable conveying a positive view of American history,” the letter said
This summer, the administration ordered the National Park Service to put up signs that would attempt to discredit the National Museum of American History
Throughout the pressure campaign, many have praised Bunch for sheltering the museums from the worst of it

Shanita Brackett, the current acting director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, told our colleague Clint Smith earlier this year that Bunch has set an example in tough times. “What he’s taught us over the last 14 months is not to be afraid, not to run,” Brackett said

Bunch had become more direct in standing up for the institution in recent months, telling CNN’s Christiane Amanpour this summer that he believes “it’s our job to tell an accurate, complex, and truthful history,” and that “it scares me when people aren’t brave enough to face their history.” Still, Bunch’s legacy goes beyond holding the line between a beloved American institution and an overbearing president

Bunch first joined the institution in 1978, starting at the Air and Space Museum, and he later took on a number of roles at the American History Museum from 1989 to 2000, including associate director of curatorial affairs
After serving as the president of the Chicago Historical Society, he returned in 2005 to the Smithsonian to build the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which opened in 2016
Under his watch, two more museums were authorized by Congress: the American Women’s History Museum and the National Museum of the American Latino

Both have faced political roadblocks; the regents recently voted to open the Latino museum in a prominent building on the National Mall that the Smithsonian already controls in order for it to move forward without having to rely on Congress or the Trump administration to grant it a new site

At the town hall today, Bunch cited the plans for the new museums, the return of pandas to the National Zoo, and the celebrations for the country’s 250th birthday as among his proudest accomplishments

A show he co-curated, likely his final for the Smithsonian, was mounted at the Smithsonian Castle this summer, offering a subtle rejoinder to those who think history is a finished story, meant only for finding glory

The framing of this show for the country’s birthday, according to its introductory text, was Thomas Jefferson’s urging that the newly formed United States be a nation “in pursuit.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: The Novel That Looks Death in the Eye
excerpt: The human brain has a method for dealing with the intrinsic fear of death
body: The human brain has a method for dealing with the intrinsic fear of death
Terror-management theory, which builds on the work of the cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker , explains that the psyche handles this fear in a variety of ways
Many people either escape reality or adopt a belief system that promises immortality: so on the one hand, sex, drugs, or entertainment; on the other, religion, fame, or careerism
Or we might immerse ourselves in family, or culture—something that imbues life with meaning
Otherwise, the theory goes, we would be cognitively immobilized by impending doom
In her gut-twisting third novel, Switzy , Emma Cline does not abide by the tenets of terror management
Instead, she pulls death out from behind the curtain and forces her readers to look it in the eye for more than 300 pages
Switzy follows the final few days in the life of David Hastings, a former high-flying executive who’s been forced into retirement, and obsolescence, by an Alzheimer’s diagnosis
He has taken advantage of Switzerland’s right-to-die laws , paying the fees (a paltry sum for a wealthy man) and filling out the required paperwork
Now he’ll swallow some barbiturates and die in an impersonal room just outside Zurich, far from his family and his home in America
Cline’s approach is merciless—not toward David, for whom she shows tenderness and grace, but toward the reader, who will be nearly flattened by this novel
Or so I sincerely hope, because death ought to flatten us once in a while
Switzy begins mid-flight, as David hurtles across the Atlantic in a friend’s private jet
Accompanied by Cody—a former corporate underling who now functions as David’s caretaker, body man, and secretary—he lands first in London
There, he has dinner with his only child, an emotionally distant daughter who doesn’t know about her father’s decline, let alone his upcoming euthanasia
David tours a museum, visits his grandson, reboards the plane for his final flight, to Zurich; he dazedly lets Cody steer him around as a parent would guide a toddler
The younger man negotiates the intricacies of the world on David’s behalf, buffering him from the demands of day-to-day life—buying a museum ticket, sending a text message, procuring beverages
David needs the help: He is at times absent in his own mind

As rendered by Cline in a wandering, dreamlike style, this becomes a startling and eerie phenomenon—like the moment you realize you’ve been driving for miles but don’t recall anything about the journey
Far from experiencing the blissful ignorance that some people might project onto dementia patients , David is all too aware that his brain has locked away basic memories and social customs

He writes his grandson’s name, Rainer, in a notebook so he can recall it; a clock “in big kindergarten letters” informs him of the date and time each morning; he stares too long at someone in the museum and provokes his annoyance
And he sees each gap, knows that it signals another loss. “Work,” he thinks as he chews a croissant, “everything seemed like work
Even these good things—even this buttered mouthful.” [ Read: A different way to think about medicine’s most stubborn enigma ] The first half of Switzy crawls by, but it feels achingly necessary
This is time the way David experiences it, slowed down and sometimes skipped over: Alzheimer’s novels are rare, and those told from the patient’s point of view are even rarer
Cline, always a graceful stylist , employs a kind of abbreviated modernism to leap among David’s thoughts
They skitter backwards to memories of his failed marriage and his time at a boys’ boarding school

They run in circles, around catchy sayings—such as a mnemonic about Henry VIII’s abbreviated marriages, “Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived”—that Alzheimer’s hasn’t stolen from him
And they jump ahead to the moment and manner of his death, which inches closer with every turned page
Cline’s last novel, The Guest , also followed a character who hastily approaches a reckoning

Alex, a poor and wily 22-year-old sex worker who has just been kicked out of the home of her most recent catch, Simon, has to make it through five days in the Hamptons, until she can plead to be let back into the high-end milieu of Simon’s Labor Day party
Dead-eyed and mutable, Alex, like David, is trying to put on just enough of a show to pass muster with the people around her
For her, a different kind of death awaits—complete impoverishment, and removal from a perch where she may or may not belong
Switzy raises the stakes on this kind of quest
As the novel’s second half picks up steam, so does the cadence of David’s confrontations with the fact of his looming extinction
When the plane lands in Zurich, an official comes on to inspect their passports. “David smiled to himself
It was obvious, wasn’t it? This man was Death
Why else would he know to come right onboard?” Soon after, he sees Death again as a waiter, a busboy, two restaurant patrons
On his last night, he wakes repeatedly in his hotel, checking the sky’s brightness as a sign of how much time he has left
An Omega watch advertisement catches his eye, and though he doesn’t say it, the meaning is clear: Omega is the last letter in the Greek alphabet, the universal symbol of finality
As long as David cannot stop returning to his ticking clock, neither can you

title: The Myth of Perfect Knowledge
excerpt: The modern world owes a lot to the Enlightenment, the 18th-century intellectual movement that emphasized the power of reason
body: The modern world owes a lot to the Enlightenment, the 18th-century intellectual movement that emphasized the power of reason
But the Enlightenment also created a myth: that we can get to know the objective world completely, with total clarity, as if we were looking at it from the outside
This myth is challenged by the Enlightenment’s greatest legacy—modern science
Physics—my trade, and perhaps the most objective among the sciences—questions the possibility of a full description of how things objectively are
An electron can be in a “quantum superposition,” so that to an observer, it doesn’t occupy just one location—and so can you, my reader
This does not mean that you could perceive being dislocated between two positions; as perceived by yourself, you are always in just one place
But an object’s properties may differ depending on who, or what, is looking at them—or may not even be defined at all
Properties are not simple features of things: They are relations between one thing and another
What we call “the world” is therefore only how some parts of reality manifest themselves to other parts—us, for instance
Humanity has always been aware that our understanding is partial and biased
But the fact that an objective and knowable reality is incompatible with the grammar of physics is astonishing
The Enlightenment could consider the mind as being outside the world, in an abstract realm of reason where knowledge resides
But human minds are not outside reality, watching it from its exterior
We, like everything else, are part of the very nature we study
Our knowledge is only one example of the many correlations that intertwine different parts of nature
In the early 20th century, Niels Bohr, a founder of quantum theory, realized that quantum phenomena indicate that we cannot discard our own physical nature when we observe the world
The ideal of grasping objective reality by making the observer irrelevant is incompatible with physics
We are quantum processes interacting with other quantum processes

Our knowledge is a rich but incomplete set of correlations between one piece of the world–ourselves–and the rest of it. [ Adam Frank: The truth physics can no longer ignore ] To see this fact from another point of view, consider saying “It’s raining and Ann does not know it.” This makes sense: You know that it’s raining and that Ann doesn’t

But if you replace “Ann” with a first-person pronoun, the result is odd: “It’s raining and I do not know it.” How can you declare that it’s raining if you do not know it? This observation points to the fact that every proposition can only express the knowledge of the speaker or writer
No proposition is asserted from outside reality, because there is nothing outside reality
To say “It is raining” is really to say: “I, as part of reality, know that it’s raining.” Objective statements independent of any knower are fictions
Purely objective reality is a useful myth, but only a myth
Anything said about the state of the world comes from someone’s singular perspective
This means that all of our knowledge is intrinsically uncertain
All statements have unavoidable margins of uncertainty
Indeed, we can be wrong about anything, even the basic facts of our own lives
My father grew up sure that his first name was Franco until he asked for a copy of his birth certificate and found out that my grandfather, without telling my grandma, had registered him as Giulio
Humanity has been collectively wrong over and over again
We thought the sun moved around the earth, then learned that it is the earth that orbits the sun
Great scientists are even more likely to be wrong than others, because they have the courage to try—Einstein’s published work includes many mistakes
But in science, as in daily life, we do not need certainty; being reasonably sure is good enough
If I have an airplane to catch, I will go to the airport even though I’m not totally sure that the flight will take off; if I waited for certainty, I’d never leave home

Modern science offers an enormous body of knowledge that is effective and, in many domains, far better than all the alternatives, but it gives us no absolute certainty, no ultimate story, no Truth with a capital T
Within science, there are different ways of describing the same things

A glass of water can be described in terms of physics (its mass, velocity), thermodynamics (its temperature), chemistry (there is more than just H 2 O in any glass of water), biology (bacteria swim in it), particle physics (its electrons, protons, and neutrons), psychology (“Why did I fill the glass?”), economics (its price), and more
Each account is valid in its own terms; each reflects a way in which the same object interacts with different parts of reality, from atoms to the global economy
But none exhausts an “ultimate truth” of the glass. [ Alan Lightman: The mind-body question ] The same is true for human beings
I can think of you, my reader, as a body, as a mind, or as a soul

These aren’t different entities: They are the same entity, described in different languages, using different conceptual schemes, focusing on different aspects of the same you and different ways in which you interact with other parts of reality

title: The Download: our 35 Innovators Under 35 this year

title: This founder is teaching chips how to recycle (their energy)
excerpt: Throughout the history of the computer chip, engineers have treated waste heat as an inevitable cost of a calculation
body: Throughout the history of the computer chip, engineers have treated waste heat as an inevitable cost of a calculation
Hannah Earley, however, thinks it’s a design choice
Earley, 31, is cofounder and chief technology officer of Vaire Computing, a startup building chips that recycle energy usually thrown away as heat—a strategy known as reversible computing
Ultimately, she thinks, this approach could help make data centers (and our laptops and phones) much more energy efficient
When conventional computer chips perform calculations, they erase the information they no longer need along the way, dissipating energy as heat in the process
Earley compares the approach to racing through a city only to pump the brakes at every intersection: The car loses momentum and must burn more fuel to accelerate again

Reversible computing aims to keep the momentum going—instead of erasing information from the intermediate steps in a calculation, the circuit retains it, making it possible to run the computation backward and recover some of the energy
While the idea was first proposed more than 50 years ago, it proved impractical to implement with existing transistors and circuits
Earley, though, has completely rethought the hardware needed to make energy recovery work
She designed a patent-pending type of resonator—a microscopic chip component that stores recovered energy for later reuse. “It’s really a glorified pendulum,” she says
Last year, Vaire announced a key breakthrough: a chip with a resonator that recovered more energy than it lost, even after the energy needed to power the component was taken into account

For a subfield that has existed mostly in theory, the result was proof of life. “It’s clear they have something interesting,” says Igor Markov, a researcher in electronic design automation and a former professor at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

Still, he says, the technology is quite early stage; the company will need “a series of increasingly realistic and convincing demonstrations to attract the industry support needed for commercialization.”  She gradually became convinced that the connection between information, energy, and heat could change computers forever
Earley’s journey into chip design started sooner than most
She began programming around the age of nine, starting with high-level coding for the web before digging into other programming languages like Perl and Java
She continued progressing to more and more abstract layers of computing, until she got all the way down to transistors
She eventually enrolled in a PhD program at the University of Cambridge under the computational biologist Gos Micklem
She started out studying how materials such as DNA could be used to perform calculations, but a few months in, Micklem sent her the 1999 PhD thesis of Michael Frank, a pioneer in reversible computing
Earley read it once, felt skeptical, read it again, and sat with it for a few weeks
She gradually became convinced that the connection between information, energy, and heat could change computers forever
The fascination completely redirected her PhD work

Earley studied the physical limits of computation and built software that could turn ordinary programs into reversible ones. “Eventually I wouldn’t let her put my name on any of her papers, because I felt that I couldn’t really stand up and give a proper talk about them,” Micklem recalls. “It was her stuff.” After completing her degree in 2021, Earley met Rodolfo Rosini, a technology entrepreneur and investor

The pair cofounded Vaire that same year, and the company has since raised more than $12 million, hired Frank as a senior scientist, and begun turning the vision of reversible computing into real hardware
Innovation, however, doesn’t happen overnight

During the winter of 2022 in Grinnell, Iowa, Earley spent weeks in her now-wife’s basement apartment as the wind chill outside reached roughly −40 °F, covering a whiteboard over and over again with schematics for the core piece of circuitry needed to make reversible logic work

By the time the design finally came together, after the couple had escaped the cold for Las Vegas, it felt less like an aha moment and more like a gradual wave of relief. “I’m not completely out of my depth,” she remembers feeling.  Earley and her colleagues’ next challenge is making their drastically different chip fit into familiar devices and manufacturing systems

She believes that’s where the future lies—not in further refining existing chips but in rebuilding them from the ground up with an eye toward reversibility. “I want to tackle every part of how computers are built,” Earley says, “and rethink it in these terms.”

title: This AI entrepreneur is developing agents that can plan ahead for the unexpected
excerpt: Danijar Hafner’s office in San Francisco’s SoMa district sits mostly empty
body: Danijar Hafner’s office in San Francisco’s SoMa district sits mostly empty
His brand-new startup is still in stealth mode and doesn’t even have its name on the door
On the day I visit, there’s only one other person there, and little in the way of furniture
But what it lacks in decor, it makes up for in robots
Humanoids of various shapes and sizes hang like marionettes from racks that run down the center of the wide-open space
While Hafner, 31, won’t say too much about his new venture just yet, he describes it as a continuation of his longtime work to enable AI to navigate environments it has not encountered in training
The humanoids, which he imports from China, are the next evolution of this work—and its physical embodiment
Their ability to react in previously untested scenarios will be key to getting robots into human spaces

Because if you want to send a robot into a person’s home, for example, it needs to be able to handle a floor plan and furniture it’s never seen before.  To achieve this, Hafner relies on something called model-based reinforcement learning
He develops world models—AI models designed to emulate physical reality—and trains agents within them
The agent essentially treats the model as a real-world simulation and learns how to act there
It then uses those experiences to make predictions (to dream or imagine, Hafner might say) about future outcomes

That allows agents—or the robots they’re embedded in—to navigate unfamiliar situations IRL. “I get to interact with a lot of really smart people in research at Google, and he easily sits in the top half of 1%.” Timothy Lillicrap, Google DeepMind Unlike other efforts, Hafner’s technique enables agents and the robots they control to execute massively complicated tasks without the real-world trial-and-­error training that’s traditionally been used in robotics.  Hafner grew up in a rural town in northeastern Germany, where his parents were both classical musicians
He learned programming from a neighbor, and in high school he began taking online courses about AI, which quickly developed into a passion. “I was always fascinated with how thinking works,” he says
AI offered him a way to emulate it on a computer
In 2015, as a second-year under­graduate studying engineering at Hasso Plattner Institute in Potsdam, he won a role as a student researcher at Google Brain

From there, he went on to a dozen internships and other positions at the company, including stints with Google Brain and Google DeepMind (the two have since merged under DeepMind) in the UK, Canada, and the US

He worked with industry legends including Geoffrey Hinton, who is often referred to as one of the godfathers of AI, and Ashish Vaswani, coauthor of the groundbreaking research paper “Attention Is All You Need,” which described the transformer technology used by today’s large language models

One of Hafner’s former managers and coauthors at Google, Timothy Lillicrap, describes him as a standout among standouts. “I get to interact with a lot of really smart people in research at Google, and he easily sits in the top half of 1%,” Lillicrap says. “In many cases he would build, single-­handedly, things it would take entire teams of engineers to build.” Over the years, Hafner has honed and proved his approach by pitting agents trained within his world models against popular video games
His first breakthrough was PlaNet, a model that allowed agents to execute actions by planning ahead
His Dreamer 2 was the first agent to hit human-level performance playing Atari 2600 games using a world model
Dreamer 3 was the first one to solve the Minecraft Diamond challenge—successfully mining in-game gems on its own

And Dreamer 4 went a step beyond that by learning to mine diamonds from an offline data set of recorded game-play videos, without ever interacting with the game directly.  More recently, he’s begun to migrate his agents out of the virtual world and into physical reality

His DayDreamer project used the Dreamer algorithm to let robots operate themselves in novel environments and react to new experiences (such as being pushed over) without any specific training.  Today, Hafner is working on his new startup, which he left Google DeepMind to form in the fall of 2025
Though he’s coy about his next steps, it’s clear he’s dreaming big: “I was interested in solving a problem,” he hints, “that would change the world.”

title: This founder is making cheaper, cleaner steel
excerpt: The steel industry isn’t exactly known for innovation
body: The steel industry isn’t exactly known for innovation
Very little has changed about purifying iron ore since the process was invented and commercialized in the 1850s
The majority of steelmakers melt solid iron ore at dizzyingly high temperatures inside blast furnaces, where the material reacts with gases to trigger chemical reactions that remove oxygen
It then undergoes further refining to purify it before it is made into products like rebar and car frames
The process relies on coal, and it generates roughly 7% of the carbon emissions that drive climate change—about as much as the fashion industry
Decarbonization has proved difficult: Profit margins are tight and furnaces have long service lives, making investment tough to justify
Now Laureen Meroueh may have found a way to clean up steelmaking without driving up the price
Meroueh, the founder of Hertha Metals, invented a new furnace that simplifies the chemistry behind the process
Her method turns iron ore into refined liquid steel in a single step, and it swaps coal for natural gas
Together, those changes slash emissions by at least half, she says, and cut costs by 25% compared with steelmaking business as usual

If it catches on, the tech could be transformative. “There’s huge value in reducing the size of this production system,” says Iryna Zenyuk, director of the National Fuel Cell Research Center at the University of California, Irvine. “They’re massive

They’re inefficient and require a lot of energy input, so even if they just save energy efficiency, that’s already a big step.” Hertha’s approach focuses on what it can fix about the steel industry now, as opposed to waiting around for a zero-carbon system
Still, it’s a risky endeavor, but pushing limits isn’t new for Meroueh
At 12 she was accepted into a pilot program to take college-­level courses through Florida Atlantic University in lieu of a traditional secondary education
She was immediately drawn to engineering and explored topics including calculus and ocean wave energy

Despite the rigorous coursework, she would spend hours sitting in trees and surfing, which fostered a deep appreciation for nature and a desire to safeguard it. “I don’t know how you can’t be drawn toward trying to help protect that,” she says.  Now 34, Meroueh has let that passion inform her professional goals
After finishing her PhD in mechanical engineering at MIT, she led a green hydrogen startup before founding Hertha in 2022

A first-generation Lebanese-American from an entrepreneurial family, she saw starting her own company as a typical path. “Seeing how common it is to take that jump to start your own business is what made me feel like ‘This is normal,’” she explains on a video call from her office at Hertha’s pilot plant in Conroe, Texas, just north of Houston

That facility can produce one metric ton of steel per day. “One ton per day is a big metric for steel,” says Rajesh Swaminathan, a partner at Khosla Ventures, one of the company’s investors. (Hertha had raised about $20 million in funding as of July 2026.)  Swaminathan says the company’s scale-up is “impressive,” especially given how little the team has spent
Competitors, he notes, have created far less steel with $50 million or $100 million in funding
Hertha’s approach focuses on what it can fix about the industry now, as opposed to waiting around for a zero-carbon system

While other approaches to making green steel center on using hydrogen to free oxygen from iron ore—a method that could one day cut or eliminate emissions—Meroueh says Hertha is content for the time being with a continued reliance on fossil fuels, mainly to keep costs down

The current Hertha plant could eventually switch to a fully decarbonized system without drastically changing the hardware, she says, if hydrogen becomes more affordable.  In the meantime, plans are underway to expand into a new plant next to the existing one
The facility is slated to produce 10,000 metric tons of high-purity steel per year and should reach full capacity by the end of 2027
By 2030, Meroueh believes, Hertha can up its output to 500,000 metric tons per year with the addition of a third site
That’s only a fraction of the approximately 80 million metric tons of steel produced annually in the US, but Zenyuk says making even one metric ton is still an achievement

In Meroueh’s mind, the world isn’t going to outgrow its need for steel, so she’s asking another question: “How can we be smarter about how we make things … so that it’s also not going to harm us in the long term?”

title: This geneticist’s age-reversal tech could help restore sight
excerpt: Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is obsessed with aging
body: Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is obsessed with aging
As he steps outside the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, his aviator glasses darken automatically in the sun
A great-aunt in China, the story goes, was killed crossing a road because she couldn’t see oncoming traffic
And Lu’s own 23andMe test came back with a mutation for macular degeneration, a top cause of vision loss in old age

Exposure to bright sunlight is another risk factor—thus the shades. “They protect me,” he says. “Plus, they look cool.” Lu, 34, works on gene therapies to prevent age-related vision loss. “I think the eye is a really unique system to study aging and rejuvenation,” he says. “I could give a whole presentation.” Pushing up my reading glasses, I lean in to listen
Lu is behind one of the coolest results in rejuvenation science—and in eye research
In 2018, while earning his PhD at Harvard Medical School, he used an age-reversal technique called reprogramming to repair the optic nerves of mice
He crushed the nerves, blinding the animals, and then injected the cells with a gene therapy meant to restore them to a youthful state
Sixteen days later, the nerves were growing back, their axons showing up through a microscope as spidery orange filaments

As hype around age reversal swirls, Lu has been busy in the lab searching for what he calls “the next generation of rejuvenation therapies.” The head of that lab, the longevity scientist David Sinclair, remembers when Lu texted him the pictures: “He asked me, ‘What do you see here?’ And I said, ‘I see the future.’” Later tests carried out in a box with rotating bars of light showed the mice were tracking the changes
This year, nearly the exact genetic therapy Lu created for mice entered human clinical trials
On June 9, the startup Life Biosciences, which Sinclair cofounded and in which Lu owns a small stake, announced it had injected the treatment into the eye of a person with glaucoma

A headline in the New York Times suggested the technology could “change humanity.” Posters on X gushed, with one declaring that “the fountain of youth is here.” “It’s remarkable that what he developed as a student is now going into humans,” says Sinclair of the treatment, now called ER-100. “It’s barely even changed since he built it.” Reprogramming refers to an age-­restoring process that takes place inside an embryo
It’s why babies are born young, not old: The DNA they’ve inherited from their parents has been scrubbed and reset
In 2006, Japanese researchers showed they could cause the process to occur in the lab by introducing just four key genes, known by the acronym OSKM
Add these to a cell from a 100-year-old and it will turn into a stem cell that acts as if it was plucked from an embryo
But we don’t want to turn people into blobs of stem-cell protoplasm
Lu figured out a way to control the effect
He trimmed the list of genes to just OSK—leaving out M, for Myc , the one most likely to cause dangerous changes like cancer
His extra flash of insight was that reprogramming could be tested on the optic nerve; the eye is particularly accessible
Lu’s result, published in Nature in 2020, helped set off an investment rush
Since then, US tech billionaires have placed huge bets on private companies like Altos Labs and NewLimit to explore reprogramming and anti-aging medicine

The day I spoke with Lu, he’d spent the morning meeting with the business magnate Zhong Shanshan, one of China’s richest people.   Still, as hype around age reversal swirls, Lu has been notably absent from the public conversation

He’s been busy in the lab searching for what he calls “the next generation of rejuvenation therapies.” With a sigh, Lu describes the grueling effort over the last six years to understand what OSK really does
The treatment remains toxic to many cell types, and he says it’s becoming obvious that different factors drive aging in each kind
This year, for example, he identified a gene responsible for protecting the retina from damage by free radicals—the main cause of age-­related macular degeneration
While Sinclair, his former boss, believes humans could live to be 200, Lu disagrees
There’s just too much that goes wrong as we age
His work with OSK, he says, was more a proof of concept than a silver bullet
But it did change the conversation. “Six years ago, you couldn’t talk about rejuvenation
We didn’t use that word—there was pushback,” Lu tells me. “But I think people have accepted the concept that you can really reverse molecular age.”

title: You can’t shield kids from scary news – here’s what ‘Sesame Street’ and other children’s shows did after 9/11
url:
<title>You can’t shield kids from scary news – here’s what ‘Sesame Street’ and other children’s shows did after 9/11</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758286/original/file-20260907-50-p3kjs1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=119%2C52%2C5546%2C3697&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Mourners on Staten Island watch a funeral procession for a firefighter killed during the 9/11 terrorist attacks.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-mourners-as-they-watch-a-funeral-procession-on-news-photo/2291894301?adppopup=true">Peter Turnley/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On back-to-school night in 2005, I eagerly entered my youngest child’s first grade classroom. The walls were festooned with brightly colored responses to the prompt: “Draw something you remember.”</p>

<p>I scanned for my son’s picture and was shocked when I encountered his drawing: an airplane flying into New York’s World Trade Center.</p>

<p>“I saw the picture you drew up on the bulletin board,” I said to him later that night. “Do you really remember seeing planes flying into the twin towers?” </p>

<p>He looked me in the eyes and replied, “No, Mommy. But I do remember you crying.”</p>

<p>My son was not quite 2 years old on on Sept. 11, 2001. As a mother, I despaired to learn that my own reaction to that day’s tragedies had stuck with him so viscerally. <a href="https://www.juliedobrow.com/about">As a professor and researcher of children’s media</a>, I shouldn’t have been surprised.</p>

<p>My son’s memory was likely influenced not just by my emotional reaction but by the media around him that his parents and siblings consumed in the weeks and years after the attacks – a mix of TV news and content geared toward kids.</p>

<p>More than two decades later, children have many more ways and more platforms to encounter frightening images and stories, often without an adult nearby to help them make sense of what they see. But the ways children’s programming such as “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0063951/">Sesame Street</a>” responded to 9/11 offer a useful lesson: Rather than trying to shield children completely from disturbing events, adults can help them process what they’ve seen in honest, reassuring and age-appropriate ways.</p>

<h2>You can’t shield kids from what’s happening</h2>

<p><a href="https://icacamsite.wordpress.com/in-the-spotlight/joanne-cantor/">Psychologist Joanne Cantor</a> was one of the first to study what scares children about news and how they respond to it. </p>

<p>She concluded that <a href="https://www.sagepub.com/shop/buy-a-book/handbook-of-children-and-the-media-2-234728">what frightens children varies by their developmental stage</a>. Younger children tend to notice and respond to stories about natural disasters and tragedies about kids or animals. Older children are afraid of stories focusing on personal injury and physical destruction, kidnapping, disease and violence. Teens express fear of stories about random acts of violence, natural disasters and foreign conflicts.</p>

<p>Since Cantor first published her groundbreaking research in the 1980s, kids’ media environments have changed dramatically, with more channels, screens and platforms broadcasting images and videos of natural disasters, violence and tragedies from around the world.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A child's note expressing sorrow for the victims of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, accompanied by a drawing of two planes smashing into two towers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=435&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=435&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=435&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=546&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=546&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758285/original/file-20260907-50-gf6b58.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=546&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/01463373.2012.669340">One study</a> found that young children’s exposure to news is often accidental but lasting, with many children recalling distressing images long after the fact. <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4803729/">Another one</a> found that violent news images take a cumulative toll on children’s mental and emotional health. And <a href="https://izi.br.de/english/publication/televizion/33_2020_E/Goetz_Mendel_Lemish-Children_COVID-19_and_the_media.pdf">an international survey</a> of over 4,000 children from 42 countries found that over half had been scared by stories about the COVID-19 pandemic.</p>

<p>More recently, the children’s media nonprofit <a href="https://www.commonsensemedia.org/kids-action/articles/our-new-research-shows-where-kids-get-their-news-and-how-they-feel-about-it">Common Sense Media</a> surveyed hundreds of children ranging in age from 8 to 18 and found that what kids are seeing and hearing in the news frequently makes them feel scared, sad, angry or depressed.</p>

<h2>Children’s TV takes a delicate approach</h2>

<p>On and after 9/11, millions of children like my son either saw the images of terrorist attacks or were near adults who reacted to them.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NUVhTEa7qD8">According to “Sesame Street” producer Lewis Bernstein</a>, when the 9/11 terrorist attacks happened, most of the episodes for the forthcoming season were already written. Yet writers and producers knew that children were not oblivious – that even the 2- to 4-year-olds comprising the core “Sesame Street” audience had some sense of what was going on. </p>

<p>In response, the show’s producers collaborated with experts to create additional episodes that would address children’s fears.</p>

<p>In 2002, Rosemarie Truglio, vice president of education and research for “Sesame Street,” <a href="https://www.tvguide.com/news/sesame-street-tackles-41984">explained how the show’s approach</a> was to meet children where they were developmentally. </p>

<p>“Sesame Street” had already helped children process their fears through classic episodes such as “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CnOuMJAea1Q">Grover’s Fear of the Dark</a>.” Researchers knew part of what scared children on 9/11 were the loud sirens and the fact that trusted figures such as firefighters and police officers were hurt.</p>

<p>So the episode they developed in response to 9/11 made no mention of the terrorist attacks and instead centered on <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6Z6njK-LGs">a fire at Hooper’s Store</a>. Elmo is frightened by the noise of the fire alarm and subsequent sirens. The protective gear that the firefighters are wearing also scares him. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/q6Z6njK-LGs?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">“Sesame Street” never mentioned 9/11 directly, but its segments addressed fears the attacks may have instilled in children.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Fortunately, a kind and kid-savvy firefighter named Bill speaks to Elmo about his fears and invites him to visit the firehouse. There, he dispels some of Elmo’s concerns and dispenses advice about what children can do if they are ever in a similar situation. </p>

<p>The PBS show “Arthur” <a href="https://www.pbs.org/about/about-pbs/blogs/news/pbs-remembers-september-11-july-26-2002/">took a similar approach</a>: Its two-part episode “<a href="https://arthur.fandom.com/wiki/April_9th">April 9</a>” centers on a fire at Arthur’s school. It makes no mention of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks but explores how Arthur, Sue Ellen, Binky and Buster each process the school fire differently.</p>

<p>“Zoom,” the popular PBS live-action variety show, was geared toward older kids. Just 10 days after 9/11, they aired a special half-hour episode called “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PQ94u9gzqro">America’s Kids Respond</a>.” The seven cast members, all between the ages of 9 and 14, shared their thoughts, fears and feelings. Advisers knew their audience needed more than hearing other kids talk about their feelings. So they made sure the cast also discussed <a href="https://theconversation.com/25-years-after-911-what-disasters-reveal-about-americans-ability-to-reconnect-290287">constructive things kids could do</a>, such as helping with food donations or clothing drives for affected families.</p>

<p>A year later, “Zoom” followed up with another special, “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcgW2At4vvM">America’s Kids Remember</a>,” where cast members talked about how they had coped in the months after the attacks. They also read mail from viewers, including some letters written by kids who had been targeted by anti-Muslim slurs. The episode included a segment in which a cast member visited a girl in lower Manhattan whose school had been damaged. The girl explained how she was able to cope through her art and activism.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/fFPEOI1HJQU?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A promotional clip for a special episode of “Zoom,” “America’s Kids Remember,” which aired in September 2002.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What’s a parent to do?</h2>

<p>In 2001, most children under 8 were watching <a href="https://www.kff.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/kids-media-the-new-millennium-fact-sheet.pdf">approximately 3.5 hours per day of television or videos on VHS</a>. </p>

<p>Today, <a href="https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/2025-common-sense-census-web-2.pdf">Common Sense Media reports</a> that the amount of time kids spend watching television or videos is similar, but their total media exposure is far greater, thanks to mobile platforms and different types of media.</p>

<p>In a world where extreme weather events often lead local news, natural disasters routinely take place, and school shootings and acts of political violence have become all too common, parents might naturally try to shield children from these stories. </p>

<p>But young children pick up on the news and on cues from their parents, even when we don’t think they do.</p>

<p>There are many things parents and teachers can do to help mitigate children’s fears and anxieties from what they see on the news. Recognize some of the <a href="https://sesameworkshop.org/resources/coping-with-fear/">signs your child might be feeling anxious</a>, such as sleep problems, avoidance of activities or doomscrolling. Experts suggest answering children’s questions honestly without necessarily relaying all of the gory details. It’s also OK to say, “I don’t know.”</p>

<p>Some of the lessons from how children’s TV dealt with 9/11 still apply.</p>

<p>Young children can also benefit from adults reassuring them that they are safe, by encouraging them to process a piece of news through <a href="https://www.naeyc.org/resources/pubs/yc/fall2023/story-circles">play or art</a>, and helping children by giving them language to express their questions and fears.</p>

<p>With older children and teenagers, <a href="https://www.npr.org/2019/04/24/716704917/when-the-news-is-scary-what-to-say-to-kids">experts suggest avoiding labels</a>, such as blaming something on “the bad guys.” It’s important to give kids facts and context and provide them with resources to answer their questions. Older children can benefit from outlets to express their concerns and feel agency, whether through journaling or art, or <a href="https://www.natgeokids.com/uk/parents/how-to-talk-to-kids-about-scary-news/">the kind of volunteerism</a> promoted on “Zoom.”</p>

<p>Finally, it’s important to acknowledge and explain our own emotions to our children, as I learned on that back-to-school night nearly two decades ago.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289470/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
