<title>Huachuma, the Andean psychedelic cactus, is drawing Western seekers and raising ethical questions</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757605/original/file-20260902-60-be2vft.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C338%2C2053%2C1368&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Huachuma, an Andean cactus better known as San Pedro, has been used for centuries in healing ceremonies.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Starr_070320-5799_Echinopsis_pachanoi.jpg">Forest &amp; Kim Starr via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For at least two decades, <a href="https://www.iceers.org/en/articles/reports/ayahuasca-tourism-who-how-where/">thousands of Americans have been</a> going to Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil to look for ayahuasca, a psychoactive brew traditionally used in sacred ceremonies in South America. Ayahuasca contains the psychedelic compound DMT, N-Dimethyltryptamine, and researchers are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291718001356">studying its effects</a> on several conditions, including depression and addiction. </p>

<p>However, another sacred plant is quietly drawing Western seekers as well: huachuma, the Andean cactus better known as <a href="https://www.iceers.org/en/basic-info/san-pedro-basic-info/">San Pedro</a>. The plant contains mescaline, a psychoactive compound that alters perception and mood, sharpening the senses and amplifying feelings of empathy and connection.</p>

<p>Ceremonies and <a href="https://www.alternativehealinggt.com/post/why-san-pedro-huachuma-is-spreading-around-the-world">retreats are spreading</a> across the U.S., Latin America and Europe into the thousands, as researchers take a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acsptsci.1c00018">fresh look at mescaline’s effects</a> on depression, anxiety and addiction. </p>

<p>The Conversation asked <a href="https://cshe.berkeley.edu/news/welcom-pardis-mahdavi-new-director-ela">Pardis Mahdavi</a>, a medical anthropologist who conducts research on psychedelics, to explain what huachuma is, why seekers are turning to it, and what ethical questions come with its growing popularity. </p>

<h2>1. What is huachuma?</h2>

<p>Huachuma, whose Latin name is <em>Echinopsis pachanoi</em>, is a tall cactus that grows along the spine of the Andes, the mountain range on South America’s western side. Chemists know it as a <a href="https://www.iceers.org/en/basic-info/san-pedro-basic-info/">natural source of mescaline</a>, the same psychoactive compound found in peyote. While the chemistry of the two cacti is nearly identical, the experiences they offer, how they are served and why they are consumed are different. </p>

<p>People in the Andes have used huachuma to heal physical illnesses and treat mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety for a long time. Cactus remains found in a Peruvian cave suggest use stretching back perhaps 8,000 years. At some point before roughly 1300 B.C.E. the <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16625512/">plant was carved</a> in stone at <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2425125122">Chavín de Huántar</a>, a 3,000-year-old ceremonial complex in the northern highlands of Peru, cradled in the hands of a fanged deity. </p>

<p>In the healing traditions of northern Peru, curanderos, or traditional healers, usually train through years of apprenticeship, often within family lineages. They still <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16625512/">work with the plant through the mesa</a>, an altar ceremony in which the healer drinks the brew in order to see the nature of a patient’s suffering. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/oDszI_93l1Y?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The rituals performed in the healing ceremony are necessary in the traditions of Peru.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What strikes me most, after years of studying these traditions, is the pace. In the case of ketamine, an anesthetic that U.S. clinics now <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archive/ndic/pubs4/4769/index.htm">offer legally</a> as a fast-acting treatment for depression, an infusion takes about an hour; a person can drive home the same afternoon after taking ketamine.</p>

<p>Huachuma keeps a different clock. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41386-023-01607-2">one controlled trial</a>, mescaline’s effects lasted about 11 hours on average, more than double <a href="https://theconversation.com/psilocybin-mushrooms-are-going-mainstream-but-scientific-research-and-regulation-lag-behind-277472">psilocybin’s</a> five. </p>

<p>A huachuma ceremony takes a full day. The bitter tea is drunk in the morning, and the effects arrive slowly, over an hour or two, then build through the afternoon. Participants walk, rest, talk and eat together before the ceremony closes near sunset.</p>

<p>The pace of the ceremony mirrors the pace of the plant. A cactus takes years of cultivation before it is mature enough to harvest, and turning it into tea takes the better part of a day. This is why many healers teach seekers to treat huachuma the way they would treat an elder or a teacher – someone you visit, listen to and learn from over years – rather than as a “fix me” shot.</p>

<p>A young herbalist I visited this summer near the California border would not discuss her tea-making until she had walked us through her garden, introducing her plants one by one. “First, we meet the plants,” she said. “You must know them over years, to honor the cactus in order to honor those you heal.” </p>

<h2>2. What has prompted Western seekers to turn to it?</h2>

<p>Part of the answer is the broader psychedelic renaissance: More people than ever are seeking out plant teachers, and research is beginning to catch up. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acsptsci.1c00018">One large survey</a> of people who had used mescaline found that most reported lasting improvements in conditions such as depression and anxiety after their experiences. </p>

<p>Over the past three years I have interviewed hundreds of seekers in ceremonies and retreat spaces from Arizona to Mexico to Costa Rica: veterans, police officers, CEOs, nurses, people carrying grief or diagnoses that conventional <a href="https://doi.org/10.1192/bjb.2023.25">treatment has not touched</a>. Many came to huachuma after trying nearly everything else: talk therapy, antidepressants, silent retreats, other psychedelics. </p>

<p>What draws them are few things: Huachuma takes you out of your head. It quiets the mind’s constant running commentary: the self-doubt, the criticism, the planning, the to-do lists. The shamans I have spoken with like to say that the word huachuma itself translates to “without head.” In the words of a former special forces operative: “With huachuma, it’s less about thought, and more about feeling.” And when the head quiets, the heart opens.</p>

<p>Researchers describe MDMA, the synthetic compound better known as ecstasy, as an “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2010.08.003">empathogen</a>” because it increases feelings of empathy and closeness; <a href="https://nmindjournal.com/effects-of-huachuma-as-measured-by-qeeg-pre-post-and-during-experience/">huachuma opens the same territory</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black kettle with a red lid sits beside a pot of boiling water containing a plant." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=397&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=397&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=397&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=499&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=499&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757778/original/file-20260903-50-zn21c4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=499&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Tea being prepared from San Pedro.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/san-pedro-est-le-nom-local-du-trichocerus-pachanoi-cactus-news-photo/945695284?adppopup=true">Patrick De Wilde/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Where ayahuasca ceremonies typically <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6007657/">happen at night</a> – each participant lying down inside a private journey of visions, tears and purging – huachuma ceremonies happen in daylight. People walk the trails and gardens around the ceremony site, often in pairs. They sit in circles telling stories and share a meal as the tea wears off.</p>

<p>Additionally, huachuma is gentler than most of its cousins – in ceremony circles it is often called “the grandfather” because the lore goes that grandfathers are known for spoiling their loved ones while offering gentle guidance. While seekers I interview describe a psilocybin journey as “seven years of therapy compressed into seven hours of mirrors screaming at you,” huachuma is a different kind of encounter.</p>

<p>Mescaline rarely produces the otherworldly visions people expect from psychedelics. Instead, participants stay on their feet, able to walk, talk and reflect the entire time, and that subtlety opens space for self-excavation: grief examined, old decisions revisited, at <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10508619.2022.2139502">a pace a person can actually absorb</a> . </p>

<p>None of this means huachuma is safe for everyone. Mescaline <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16349">raises heart rate</a> and blood pressure. It is <a href="https://www.iceers.org/en/basic-info/san-pedro-basic-info/">not advised</a> for people with cardiovascular conditions, certain psychiatric histories or on some medications. It remains a Schedule 1 controlled substance in the U.S., which means its use, even medicinal, is technically illegal even though the cactus itself is legal to grow. </p>

<p>A homemade brew has no standard dose, and potency varies from cactus to cactus. This is one reason untrained facilitators are genuinely dangerous. A skilled server screens participants for health risks, knows the strength of what they are pouring and stays present for all 10 or more hours. </p>

<h2>What are the ethics of using huachuma so it respects Indigenous knowledge and tradition?</h2>

<p>As <a href="https://theconversation.com/authentic-ayahuasca-rituals-sought-by-tourists-often-ignore-indigenous-practices-and-spiritual-grounding-231907">ayahuasca went global</a>, luxury retreats charged thousands of dollars, untrained facilitators set up shop, and ceremonies were stripped of the songs, diets and community obligations that gave them meaning. Indigenous communities that developed the practice saw little of the money. A sacred plant became a wellness product.</p>

<p>The shamans I have interviewed hold clear, consistent beliefs about how to serve huachuma ethically, and for them the work begins long before anyone drinks. “You must grow it,” one told me. You learn the delicate, lengthy process of <a href="http://doi.org/10.1016/j.forc.2025.100659">preparing the tea</a> or the powder: pulling out the thorns, spending hours distilling the flesh into liquid, replanting the arms of the plant. San Pedro grows in columns, called arms, and ethical growers replant a cutting for every arm they harvest, so the <a href="https://tripsitter.substack.com/p/grow-tall-san-pedro">plant outlives the serving</a>. </p>

<p>Honoring the lineage also means apprenticing with teachers in the tradition rather than learning from the internet; sourcing cacti from growers rather than stripping wild stands; and crediting the tradition openly, by naming your teachers and acknowledging the practice as Andean rather than presenting it as your own invention. It also means sending support back toward the Andean communities that kept it alive. </p>

<p>“Above all, you take your time,” a healer in San Diego told me. “With huachuma, hurry is its own form of disrespect.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290218/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Huachuma, an Andean cactus better known as San Pedro, has been used for centuries in healing ceremonies

Forest & Kim Starr via Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA For at least two decades, thousands of Americans have been going to Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil to look for ayahuasca, a psychoactive brew traditionally used in sacred ceremonies in South America
Ayahuasca contains the psychedelic compound DMT, N-Dimethyltryptamine, and researchers are studying its effects on several conditions, including depression and addiction
However, another sacred plant is quietly drawing Western seekers as well: huachuma, the Andean cactus better known as San Pedro
The plant contains mescaline, a psychoactive compound that alters perception and mood, sharpening the senses and amplifying feelings of empathy and connection
Ceremonies and retreats are spreading across the U.S., Latin America and Europe into the thousands, as researchers take a fresh look at mescaline’s effects on depression, anxiety and addiction

The Conversation asked Pardis Mahdavi , a medical anthropologist who conducts research on psychedelics, to explain what huachuma is, why seekers are turning to it, and what ethical questions come with its growing popularity. 1
What is huachuma? Huachuma, whose Latin name is Echinopsis pachanoi , is a tall cactus that grows along the spine of the Andes, the mountain range on South America’s western side
Chemists know it as a natural source of mescaline , the same psychoactive compound found in peyote
While the chemistry of the two cacti is nearly identical, the experiences they offer, how they are served and why they are consumed are different
People in the Andes have used huachuma to heal physical illnesses and treat mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety for a long time
Cactus remains found in a Peruvian cave suggest use stretching back perhaps 8,000 years

At some point before roughly 1300 B.C.E. the plant was carved in stone at Chavín de Huántar , a 3,000-year-old ceremonial complex in the northern highlands of Peru, cradled in the hands of a fanged deity
In the healing traditions of northern Peru, curanderos, or traditional healers, usually train through years of apprenticeship, often within family lineages
They still work with the plant through the mesa , an altar ceremony in which the healer drinks the brew in order to see the nature of a patient’s suffering
The rituals performed in the healing ceremony are necessary in the traditions of Peru
What strikes me most, after years of studying these traditions, is the pace

In the case of ketamine, an anesthetic that U.S. clinics now offer legally as a fast-acting treatment for depression, an infusion takes about an hour; a person can drive home the same afternoon after taking ketamine
In one controlled trial , mescaline’s effects lasted about 11 hours on average, more than double psilocybin’s five
The bitter tea is drunk in the morning, and the effects arrive slowly, over an hour or two, then build through the afternoon
Participants walk, rest, talk and eat together before the ceremony closes near sunset
The pace of the ceremony mirrors the pace of the plant
A cactus takes years of cultivation before it is mature enough to harvest, and turning it into tea takes the better part of a day
This is why many healers teach seekers to treat huachuma the way they would treat an elder or a teacher – someone you visit, listen to and learn from over years – rather than as a “fix me” shot

A young herbalist I visited this summer near the California border would not discuss her tea-making until she had walked us through her garden, introducing her plants one by one. “First, we meet the plants,” she said. “You must know them over years, to honor the cactus in order to honor those you heal.” 2
What has prompted Western seekers to turn to it? Part of the answer is the broader psychedelic renaissance: More people than ever are seeking out plant teachers, and research is beginning to catch up
One large survey of people who had used mescaline found that most reported lasting improvements in conditions such as depression and anxiety after their experiences

Over the past three years I have interviewed hundreds of seekers in ceremonies and retreat spaces from Arizona to Mexico to Costa Rica: veterans, police officers, CEOs, nurses, people carrying grief or diagnoses that conventional treatment has not touched
Many came to huachuma after trying nearly everything else: talk therapy, antidepressants, silent retreats, other psychedelics
What draws them are few things: Huachuma takes you out of your head
It quiets the mind’s constant running commentary: the self-doubt, the criticism, the planning, the to-do lists

The shamans I have spoken with like to say that the word huachuma itself translates to “without head.” In the words of a former special forces operative: “With huachuma, it’s less about thought, and more about feeling.” And when the head quiets, the heart opens
Researchers describe MDMA, the synthetic compound better known as ecstasy, as an “ empathogen ” because it increases feelings of empathy and closeness; huachuma opens the same territory

<title>Could you survive The Oregon Trail? An emergency medicine doctor offers tips on how to not die in the great outdoors</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756359/original/file-20260826-50-tp5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">You might not die of dysentery on the trail these days, but there is still plenty of danger outdoors.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/city-of-rocks-idaho-royalty-free-image/1218117306">Different_Brian/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you grew up in the United States in the 1980s or ’90s, chances are you remember <a href="https://www.visitoregon.com/the-oregon-trail-game-online/">The Oregon Trail</a>. For many like me, it was our first computer game and our first introduction to wilderness survival. We hunted buffalo, forded rivers, broke wagon wheels and, of course, <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/23567-dysentery">learned about dysentery</a> years before Google even existed, all while hoping our group would make it to Oregon City alive.</p>

<p>Lately, the game has <a href="https://oregontrail.ws/games/the-oregon-trail/">found a second life</a>. Nostalgic social media posts, memes and updated versions of the game have introduced The Oregon Trail to a new generation while reminding millennials just how unforgiving that grainy computer screen journey could be.</p>

<p>As a physician who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=9EIdcEoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">specializes in emergency and wilderness medicine</a>, I started thinking about how much of what the game taught me about surviving in the wilderness still applies today. After all, modern hikers and campers have access to tools the pioneers could never have imagined. </p>

<p>Surprisingly, I’d argue that more lessons from The Oregon Trail hold up than you might think.</p>

<h2>Clean water is crucial</h2>

<p>The Oregon Trail game <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/23567-dysentery">made dysentery famous</a> for an entire generation. Fortunately, advances in sanitation, hand hygiene and antibiotics have made large outbreaks like those that wagon trains and military camps experienced <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.281.1.61">much less common</a>, at least in the United States.</p>

<p>That doesn’t mean gastrointestinal illnesses have disappeared. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/jtm/tax026">Traveler’s diarrhea</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/cholera-still-kills-thousands-each-year-in-places-without-clean-water-its-far-from-history-288170">cholera</a> are still an important cause of illness around the world. <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-does-raw-water-compare-to-tap-water-a-microbiologist-explains-why-the-risks-outweigh-the-benefits-246866">Untreated water</a>, poor hand hygiene and contaminated food can still derail any trip. </p>

<p>Simple habits such as purifying drinking water, washing hands before meals and after using the bathroom, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/giardia/prevention/index.html">and practicing</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1128/CMR.00052-05">good camp hygiene</a> remain some of the easiest ways to stay healthy outdoors.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Steaming pot of water on small portable stove on top of a plank of wood in a forest" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=455&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=455&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=455&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=572&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=572&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756362/original/file-20260826-50-lfhrqw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=572&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Boiling is the most reliable way to purify your water.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/boiling-water-on-gas-burner-while-camping-in-serene-royalty-free-image/2230435808">Veronika Lunina/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/prevention/water-treatment-hiking-camping-traveling.html">Water purification</a> is important with wilderness travel in the United States and in many areas of the world. There are many easy and cost-effective ways to purify water, such as boiling, filtration and treating with chemical disinfectants. Each method has its benefits and downsides. </p>

<p>Boiling is often the most accessible method. While it can kill bacteria, viruses and parasites, it will not remove <a href="https://www.epa.gov/ccl/types-drinking-water-contaminants">water contaminants</a> such as heavy metals, including lead and arsenic, or industrial contamination such as pesticides. Consider boiling your water for <a href="https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water">at least one to three minutes</a>, depending on your altitude, to purify it. Water filtration is an easy option for backpackers but is less effective at removing viruses. </p>

<p>If you’re unable to boil your water, another way to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10806032231218722">ensure water safety</a> is to <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/prevention/water-treatment-hiking-camping-traveling.html">filter it</a>, then use another <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/water-disinfection-for-travelers.html">method to disinfect it</a>.</p>

<h2>Respect all waterways</h2>

<p>You may no longer have to ford the river with oxen, but rivers, lakes and other <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0160709">bodies of water present unique hazards</a> that outdoor adventure enthusiasts can overlook. </p>

<p>Moving water can be more dangerous than people realize. Even the best swimmers can drown in <a href="https://www.weather.gov/news/211309-7ripcurrent">rip currents</a>.  </p>

<p><a href="https://www.fs.usda.gov/visit/know-before-you-go/water-safety">Cross bodies of water</a> only when absolutely necessary. Avoid any water crossings after recent rainfall, as the water level often rises and the current can be faster and stronger. Submerged objects – rocks, fallen trees and other debris – as well as changing weather, flash flooding and strong currents can make crossing more dangerous.</p>

<p>If possible, use a <a href="https://usace.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16021coll11/id/1657/">Coast Guard-approved life jacket</a> when you’re crossing water or on a boat.</p>

<h2>Be ready to go the distance</h2>

<p>It’s not just a broken wagon axle that can send a trip sideways. One thing The Oregon Trail captured well is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10806032241249126">how distance</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/emj.2007.047654">changes everything</a>. A sprained ankle in a city usually means an inconvenient trip home or to the doctor, but a sprained ankle 5 miles from the trailhead may mean that someone will need to carry you. The same is true for other common wilderness concerns, such as dehydration, heat illness, infections or even blisters.</p>

<p>Preparation is about packing a first aid kit and <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/travel-for-work-other/adventure-travel.html">thinking ahead</a>. Ask yourself what you would do if your hike took twice as long as expected or if you unexpectedly had to spend the night outside. Research your route and carry more food and water than you think you’ll need. Check the weather and be prepared for it to change, with extra clothing and options for rain. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Group of hikers walking through forest, away from camera" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756363/original/file-20260826-50-yr9g9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">It’s dangerous to go alone.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/friends-walking-on-forest-royalty-free-image/2193874489">FG Trade/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>No one tackled the Oregon Trail alone because it meant you would not survive. There is a lesson here in solo travel and solo mountaineering.</p>

<p>Traveling alone means that a minor injury such as a sprained ankle could mean crawling to the trailhead to call for help or waiting until you are identified as missing. If you cannot find someone to travel with you, provide an itinerary and travel location to a trusted person. Make sure they know when you should be returning and plan to check in. If you do not return as expected, they can call for help.</p>

<h2>Respect the wildlife</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3001946">Large animals</a> still pose a threat across the country. While there may be <a href="https://theconversation.com/bison-restoration-efforts-and-grazing-rights-hinge-on-one-question-are-bison-wildlife-282921">fewer bison</a> than previously seen on the Oregon Trail, animals in nature deserve respect.</p>

<p>No selfie is worth being attacked by a brown bear. If you see a dangerous wild animal, avoid approaching and immediately leave the area.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/outdoor-workers/about/venomous-snakes.html">Venomous snakes</a> are present throughout much of the United States and continue to cause <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming">significant injury and death</a> around the world. If someone is bitten, please don’t try to cut the wound or suck out the venom. Instead, keep the person calm, minimize unnecessary movement, and focus on getting them to professional medical care. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10806032261451823">Antivenom is available</a> in many major hospitals in the United States.</p>

<p>Even smaller and more docile animals such as deer and squirrels should not be fed. It is dangerous for an animal to get used to receiving food from humans. Additionally, animals carry diseases, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(12)61678-x">rabies and leptospirosis, that can be fatal</a> to people.</p>

<p>Don’t attempt to get close to any animals, no matter how calm or asleep the animal appears to be.</p>

<h2>Technology is a backup, not a plan</h2>

<p>One of the biggest differences between today’s outdoor adventures and those of the Oregon Trail is the ability to communicate. </p>

<p>Cellphones, GPS apps and emergency beacons have made it possible to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2011.05.001">call for help</a> from places that were once completely isolated. However, while those devices are incredibly valuable, they shouldn’t encourage you to take bigger risks, as help may be far away, slow to arrive, and injuries in the wilderness can be fatal. </p>

<p>Travelers can use a smartphone with GPS capacity to avoid getting lost, but downloading any needed maps for offline use can help prevent lack of service from derailing your trip. </p>

<p>Additionally, an <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/travel-for-work-other/adventure-travel.html">unlocked smartphone</a> that isn’t restricted to one carrier is a great way to store and communicate critical data, such as travel plans and copies of your medical history.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Person leaning over map spread over a rock beside a bike, plains stretching into the background" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756364/original/file-20260826-60-c217f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Having an offline map is critical when going somewhere remote.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-reading-map-while-on-bicycle-trip-in-royalty-free-image/966224454">Grant Ordelheide/Aurora Photos/Cavan via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Every environment has its own hazards</h2>

<p>The Oregon Trail travelers worried about river crossings, disease and harsh weather. Today’s hikers face different challenges depending on where they are. </p>

<p>Desert hikers may struggle with extreme heat and dehydration. Mountain travelers face rapidly changing weather, lightning and high altitude. And coastal explorers can face problems such as riptides, waves, cliffs and unexpected rocky surfaces.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2023.05.013">Altitude illness</a> is often unpredictable and can sneak up on you. Most people experience acute mountain sickness within 24 hours of ascent, developing symptoms such as headache, fatigue, nausea or problems with sleep. Any confusion, difficulty walking, shortness of breath or coughing up significant phlegm should prompt an immediate descent.</p>

<p>There are commonly used prescription medications to help prevent and treat altitude illness. The mountain will always be waiting for your next attempt.</p>

<h2>Some lessons survive every software update</h2>

<p>Part of what made The Oregon Trail game memorable is that every decision mattered. Success often depended less on luck than on planning ahead, and that lesson still applies. </p>

<p>When people ask me what one emergency medicine skill everyone should know before heading outdoors, my answer is usually preparation. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pcl.2010.02.001">Thoughtful planning</a> prevents far more emergencies than any single piece of equipment.</p>

<p>For people who spend a lot of time outdoors, I also recommend taking a <a href="https://www.coursera.org/learn/wilderness-first-aid-introduction">wilderness first aid course</a>. These courses teach practical skills to provide medical care in a wilderness environment.</p>

<p>Nature is no less powerful or unforgiving than it was on the Oregon Trail, and treating it with respect is essential. Combining advances in modern medicine with thoughtful preparation helps stack the odds in your favor so that, just as every Oregon Trail player hoped, everyone in the party makes it to the end.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288453/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: You might not die of dysentery on the trail these days, but there is still plenty of danger outdoors
Different_Brian/iStock via Getty Images Plus If you grew up in the United States in the 1980s or ’90s, chances are you remember The Oregon Trail
For many like me, it was our first computer game and our first introduction to wilderness survival
We hunted buffalo, forded rivers, broke wagon wheels and, of course, learned about dysentery years before Google even existed, all while hoping our group would make it to Oregon City alive

Nostalgic social media posts, memes and updated versions of the game have introduced The Oregon Trail to a new generation while reminding millennials just how unforgiving that grainy computer screen journey could be
As a physician who specializes in emergency and wilderness medicine , I started thinking about how much of what the game taught me about surviving in the wilderness still applies today
After all, modern hikers and campers have access to tools the pioneers could never have imagined
Surprisingly, I’d argue that more lessons from The Oregon Trail hold up than you might think
Clean water is crucial The Oregon Trail game made dysentery famous for an entire generation

Fortunately, advances in sanitation, hand hygiene and antibiotics have made large outbreaks like those that wagon trains and military camps experienced much less common , at least in the United States
That doesn’t mean gastrointestinal illnesses have disappeared
Traveler’s diarrhea and cholera are still an important cause of illness around the world
Untreated water , poor hand hygiene and contaminated food can still derail any trip
Simple habits such as purifying drinking water, washing hands before meals and after using the bathroom, and practicing good camp hygiene remain some of the easiest ways to stay healthy outdoors
Boiling is the most reliable way to purify your water
Veronika Lunina/iStock via Getty Images Water purification is important with wilderness travel in the United States and in many areas of the world
There are many easy and cost-effective ways to purify water, such as boiling, filtration and treating with chemical disinfectants
Each method has its benefits and downsides
Boiling is often the most accessible method
While it can kill bacteria, viruses and parasites, it will not remove water contaminants such as heavy metals, including lead and arsenic, or industrial contamination such as pesticides
Consider boiling your water for at least one to three minutes , depending on your altitude, to purify it
Water filtration is an easy option for backpackers but is less effective at removing viruses
If you’re unable to boil your water, another way to ensure water safety is to filter it , then use another method to disinfect it
Respect all waterways You may no longer have to ford the river with oxen, but rivers, lakes and other bodies of water present unique hazards that outdoor adventure enthusiasts can overlook
Moving water can be more dangerous than people realize
Even the best swimmers can drown in rip currents
Cross bodies of water only when absolutely necessary
Avoid any water crossings after recent rainfall, as the water level often rises and the current can be faster and stronger
Submerged objects – rocks, fallen trees and other debris – as well as changing weather, flash flooding and strong currents can make crossing more dangerous
If possible, use a Coast Guard-approved life jacket when you’re crossing water or on a boat
Be ready to go the distance It’s not just a broken wagon axle that can send a trip sideways
One thing The Oregon Trail captured well is how distance changes everything
A sprained ankle in a city usually means an inconvenient trip home or to the doctor, but a sprained ankle 5 miles from the trailhead may mean that someone will need to carry you
The same is true for other common wilderness concerns, such as dehydration, heat illness, infections or even blisters
Preparation is about packing a first aid kit and thinking ahead
Ask yourself what you would do if your hike took twice as long as expected or if you unexpectedly had to spend the night outside
Research your route and carry more food and water than you think you’ll need
Check the weather and be prepared for it to change, with extra clothing and options for rain
FG Trade/E+ via Getty Images No one tackled the Oregon Trail alone because it meant you would not survive
There is a lesson here in solo travel and solo mountaineering

<title>AI is helping ease competition for scarce space on the airwaves</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757869/original/file-20260903-50-gmszrf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8640%2C5759&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The radio airwaves are getting crowded.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/communications-tower-is-pictured-near-a-data-centre-on-news-photo/2291595679">Carl Court/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Every time you make a phone call, stream a video or connect to Wi-Fi, your device is sending and receiving invisible signals through the air. So are your baby monitor, garage door opener, your GPS, the weather-monitoring satellites and the radars keeping planes safely apart. All of these rely on the same invisible resource: the radio spectrum. </p>

<p>The demand for wireless data – driven by smartphones, video streaming and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/COMST.2023.3249835">billions of connected devices</a> – keeps growing, making available spectrum scarce. But it doesn’t have to remain that way. As an <a href="https://ece.osu.edu/people/yener.5">electrical engineer</a> who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=W6DNu0cAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">studies wireless communications</a>, I’m part of a field of research working to address the radio spectrum supply crunch.</p>

<p>The solution engineers and regulators have been developing is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/TCCN.2016.2592921">dynamic spectrum sharing</a>. The core idea is straightforward: Instead of reserving a portion of spectrum exclusively for one user forever, allow multiple users to share the same frequencies – intelligently, and with clear rules to keep them from stepping on each other’s signals.</p>

<p>Radio spectrum is at the low end of the electromagnetic spectrum, with frequencies below microwaves, light and X-rays. You can think of it as a vast collection of invisible highways, running at different frequencies, carrying signals through the air. Television, air traffic control, cellphones, remote sensing of distant stars – they all travel on different parts of this same invisible road network.</p>

<p>These communication highways <a href="https://www.tutorialspoint.com/article/the-electromagnetic-spectrum">span an enormous range</a>, from very low frequencies used for submarine communication all the way up beyond radio waves to the frequencies of visible light. Higher frequencies carry signals over shorter distances but can move more data with wider highways. Because there is only so much spectrum to go around as a matter of fundamental physics, governments have historically managed it by issuing exclusive licenses – dedicating certain highways to specific users and telling everyone else to stay off.</p>

<p>This system worked well enough for decades, especially because the highway network was sufficient for the demand. Studies measuring actual spectrum use over many years have found something surprising: Large stretches of licensed spectrum <a href="https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-228542A1.pdf">sit idle much of the time</a>. For example, a military radar system may only operate in certain locations on certain days. </p>

<p>Burgeoning demand for radio spectrum has left some of these roads clogged with traffic jams, while others nearby sit almost completely empty.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a horizontal chart overlaying a scene with a landscape at the bottom, clouds in the middle and space at the top" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=492&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=492&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757877/original/file-20260903-50-apggp6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=492&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Radio communications occupy a small portion of the electromagnetic spectrum.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Electromagnetic_spectrum,_NASA_illustration.jpg">NASA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Traffic control for radio</h2>

<p>Making dynamic spectrum sharing work requires radios that are more flexible than the fixed-frequency devices of the past. </p>

<p>Today’s smartphones and wireless devices are increasingly built on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/35.393001">software-defined radio</a> technology, meaning the frequencies they operate on can be adjusted by software rather than being locked into hardware. Think of it like a car that can switch lanes automatically rather than being stuck in one lane forever. Early researchers called the vision behind this “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-374535-4.X0001-X">cognitive radio</a>” – the idea of a radio that could sense its environment and adapt accordingly.</p>

<p>This flexibility opens the door <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/JSAC.2004.839380">to a layered approach</a> to spectrum sharing. At the top of the hierarchy sit incumbent primary users – those who hold existing rights to a frequency, such as the military or licensed broadcasters. Below them, other secondary users can access the same spectrum when and where the incumbents aren’t using it, stepping aside automatically the moment an incumbent returns.</p>

<p>A more everyday version of this kind of sharing already exists in the Wi-Fi frequencies you use at home. Multiple devices – your laptop, your phone, your smart TV – share the same spectrum without a central authority assigning each one a dedicated slot. They do this by briefly <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/TCOMM.2015.2443041">sensing whether the channel is busy</a> before transmitting, and by automatically adjusting their speed based on how crowded things get. The protocol resembles drivers at a four-way stop – informal rules that mostly work without anyone directing traffic.</p>

<p>A significant recent example of dynamic spectrum sharing in the United States is the <a href="https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/citizens-band-radio-service-cbrs">Citizens Broadband Radio Service</a>, or CBRS, operating in the 3.5 GHz frequency band. The Federal Communications Commission created a three-tier system. Incumbent users – primarily U.S. Navy radar systems – sit at the top. Businesses and organizations that pay for priority access sit in the middle. And the general public can use whatever is left over.</p>

<p>A central computer system – the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/MCOM.001.2000929">Spectrum Access System</a> – acts as a real-time traffic controller, constantly tracking where Navy radar is active and automatically coordinating access for everyone else. When a Navy ship is not using the spectrum in your area, hospitals, factories, warehouses and campuses can use it for their own private wireless networks. When the Navy needs it back, everyone else steps aside within seconds.</p>

              <span class="caption">The military has priority for using scarce radio spectrum.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Spectrum_Blitz_26_(9763811).jpg">U.S. Army photo by Cpl. Leonard Beckett</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>Getting around interference</h2>

<p>The biggest technical hurdle in spectrum sharing is interference – what happens when two signals overlap and scramble each other, like two people shouting different things in your ear at the same time. As <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/COMST.2023.3249835">more devices crowd the airwaves</a>, each with different power levels and different bandwidth needs, keeping signals from colliding becomes increasingly complex.</p>

<p>My lab and other researchers are now <a href="https://winnf-my.sharepoint.com/:b:/g/personal/admin_winnforum_org/IQCetnQ-teMQSpniVXZ6e1JNAUUD_t_iBi516vFiw3PQ_6Q?e=dUWo5O">turning to artificial intelligence for help</a>. AI can learn from experience and adapt in real time to changing conditions – deciding who transmits when, and at what power level, in ways that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/TWC.2024.3414428">older rule-based systems could not</a>. At the same time, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/TWC.2025.3646185">new challenges</a> are emerging, such as satellites and ground-based networks increasingly needing to share the same frequencies.</p>

<p>The way radio spectrum is managed may not seem like a kitchen table issue, but it shapes everything from how fast your phone loads a video to whether a factory can automate its floor, to the reliability of a rural school’s internet access. Future wireless technologies, including those that connect self-driving cars and enable remote surgery, will depend on having access to enough spectrum. Dynamic spectrum sharing is how to make room for all of it without dismantling the systems already in place.</p>

<p>The airwaves are finite. But with smarter management, they can do far more than once thought possible.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/267519/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>‘Star Trek’ and NASA have intertwined legacies – the show championed diversity and inspired generations of real space scientists</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757389/original/file-20260902-50-ipg6w7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C69%2C1041%2C694&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Gene Roddenberry, second from right, and Star Trek cast members visit the Space Shuttle Enterprise in 1976 with NASA Administrator James C. Fletcher, left.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.nasa.gov/history/50-years-of-nasa-and-star-trek-connections/">NASA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“Star Trek” began as a television series but grew into a cultural phenomenon. </p>

<p>When it premiered in 1966, no one could have predicted that it would lead to <a href="https://www.imdb.com/list/ls563970101/">more than a dozen spinoff shows, more than a dozen movies</a> and one of the <a href="https://www.smithsonianbooks.com/store/aviation-military-history/space-craze-americas-enduring-fascination-with-real-and-imagined-spaceflight/">most enduring fandoms</a> in popular culture.</p>

<p>“Star Trek” is also unusual for its close connections to NASA, both in its storylines and in the real world. Decades of “Star Trek” adventures have ignited a love of spaceflight across generations, inspiring many who now work as space professionals.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.gvsu.edu/anthropology/dr-deana-weibel-5.htm">I’m a cultural anthropologist</a> who studies why people work in space exploration. I’ve interviewed astronomers, engineers, flight surgeons and astronauts. Although I focus more on science fact than science fiction, I’ve noticed in my interviews how much the two threads intertwine. </p>

<p>Because of this, I found myself at a “Star Trek” convention in early August 2026, just ahead of the show’s <a href="https://www.startrek.com/news/star-trek-60th-2026-fan-centric-celebrations">60th anniversary</a> on Sept. 8. The convention participants included people of widely different ages, appearances and identities. I was struck by just how much those gathered reflected the series’ values.</p>

<h2>When NASA met Star Trek</h2>

<p>In the original series, the show’s creator, Gene Roddenberry, came up with a philosophy held by the Vulcan people. He called it <a href="https://www.fanlore.org/wiki/IDIC_%28glossary_term%29">IDIC: infinite diversity in infinite combinations</a>. It suggests that an ideal society is made up of many different types, all working together. </p>

<p>It represented Roddenberry’s rejection of conformity. It also explained why the Enterprise crew included a Russian alongside Americans, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-teacher-uses-star-trek-for-difficult-conversations-on-race-and-gender-43098">Black, Japanese and female characters</a> all in positions of responsibility and authority. While many ordinary viewers absorbed “Star Trek’s” lessons of camaraderie and acceptance, those involved in real space exploration also took notice. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black-and-white photo of four characters wearing Starfleet uniforms, including two white men, an Asian man and a Black woman." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=795&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=795&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=795&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=999&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=999&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758065/original/file-20260904-50-l72hcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=999&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>

<p>Roddenberry <a href="https://schifferbooks.com/products/inspired-enterprise">established relationships with NASA personnel</a> in the early days of his series. NASA provided photographs of planetary bodies and advice about the realities of spaceflight, as well as stock footage and access to certain NASA facilities. </p>

<p>Leonard Nimoy, who played the popular character Mr. Spock, was even brought to the National Space Club’s <a href="https://www.thespacereview.com/article/4240/1">Goddard Memorial Dinner in 1967</a> as a special guest. Then-Vice President Hubert Humphrey gave the keynote speech. Afterward, though, it was Nimoy, not Humphrey, who found himself surrounded by the club’s members, including NASA employees, aerospace engineers, members of the military and government officials, all eager to meet the actor portraying the starship Enterprise’s first officer. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/how-star-trek-helped-nasa-dream-big-180976753/">The relationship between NASA and “Star Trek”</a> benefited the show by legitimizing the series. It also helped NASA by publicizing its work and depicting a positive future where its efforts to land on the Moon would eventually lead to visits to distant worlds – and amazing scientific advances like the show’s <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Treknology/WsA2DwAAQBAJ">transporter and warp drive</a>.</p>

<p>The connection between the space show and space agency was reflected in NASA’s decision to name its first space shuttle <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/history/space-shuttle-enterprise-makes-its-public-debut">Enterprise</a>, after some <a href="https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20250717-the-star-trek-space-shuttle-names-that-never-were">encouragement from the “Star Trek” fan community</a>. </p>

<h2>Inspiring astronauts</h2>

<p>In 1977, actress Nichelle Nichols, who portrayed communications officer Uhura, was <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/people-of-nasa/special-observances/nichelle-nichols-helped-nasa-break-boundaries-on-earth-and-in-space">hired to recruit for NASA</a>. The space agency had expanded its pool of astronauts to include <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/history/mercury-7-to-artemis-ii/">scientists and other “mission specialists.”</a> For the first time, an astronaut no longer needed to be a pilot to participate in a space mission.</p>

<p>NASA selected its <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/history/the-class-of-1978-and-the-flats/">first Black astronaut candidates and its first female astronaut candidates</a> in 1978. While this move toward inclusivity may not have been directly influenced by infinite diversity in infinite combinations, it was compatible with it. “Star Trek” inspired many of NASA’s future employees. In interviews for my book “<a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-ultraview-effect/hardcover">The Ultraview Effect</a>,” a quarter of the space professionals I spoke with mentioned “Star Trek” as an influence. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>An Apollo astronaut I interviewed, for instance, said he believed humans would eventually “be able to go anywhere in the universe, just like ‘Star Trek.’” </p>

<p>A young engineer who had grown up in the 1990s told me his motivation came from the “opening line of ‘Star Trek’… to explore strange new worlds.” </p>

<p>A space shuttle mission specialist emphasized Roddenberry’s decision to make the starship crew multicultural, explaining: “Today I look at the diversity of it … he was setting the stage back when it wasn’t acceptable [in order] to be acceptable!”</p>

<h2>A changing future</h2>

<p>That influence has accompanied a changing astronaut corps. </p>

<p>Both the <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/astronauts/astronaut-candidates">2025 astronaut class</a>, which for the first time included more women than men, and the <a href="https://theconversation.com/meet-the-next-four-people-headed-to-the-moon-how-the-diverse-crew-of-artemis-ii-shows-nasas-plan-for-the-future-of-space-exploration-203214">crew of Artemis II</a>, which sent the first woman, first Black astronaut and first Canadian on a lunar mission, resemble the future that “Star Trek” imagined.</p>

<p>The “Star Trek” fans at the convention I attended were even more diverse. It was clear to me that Roddenberry’s “infinite diversity in infinite combinations” isn’t just a concept from the series, but something that has become a defining value of contemporary Trek fandom. </p>

            </figcaption>

<p>One such fan, <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-World-of-Star-Trek/David-Gerrold/9781939529572">Bjo Trimble</a>, holds special status. She is <a href="https://www.startrek.com/news/bjo-trimble-the-woman-who-saved-star-trek">credited with “saving ‘Star Trek’”</a> when the series was almost canceled in 1968 after two seasons. Wearing a rainbow “IDIC” pin, she signed autographs at the <a href="https://syfysistas.com/">SyFy Sistas</a> booth, where T-shirts featuring Black “Star Trek” icons such as Uhura and Benjamin Sisko were on display. </p>

<p>However, with the Trump administration’s <a href="https://www.space.com/space-exploration/trump-orders-interim-nasa-chief-to-end-dei-initiatives">recent orders to dismantle</a> all of NASA’s diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility programs and policies, institutional support for “Star Trek’s” vision of acceptance and inclusivity, which flourishes in its fan base, is <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/03/31/nx-s1-5766544/nasa-once-touted-the-diversity-of-artemis-iis-astronauts-now-not-so-much">being undone</a>. This rollback occurred just as NASA’s crews were reaching new milestones in representing the diverse future that “Star Trek” has encouraged for decades.</p>

<p>Sixty years later, some of the diverse future that “Star Trek” imagined has become part of everyday spaceflight. Other parts of that ideal remain unfinished.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290705/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Tiny backpacks reveal the secret, sometimes circuitous migrations of small songbirds</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757256/original/file-20260901-50-rl3ax4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=462%2C485%2C3162%2C2108&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A tracker must be light enough to not weigh down a bird that weighs only as much as a spoonful of sugar.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Thor Veen</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>Squinting through my binoculars, I scanned the dense branches of a black spruce, trying my best to catch a glimpse of the thin legs of a small black, white and yellow songbird. I was on the hunt for a <a href="https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Yellow-rumped_Warbler/overview">yellow-rumped warbler</a>  – a bird affectionately called “butter-butt” by bird-watchers after the distinctive buttery yellow patch of feathers above its tail.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman in a veiled hat holds a small bird with red and yellow bands on its legs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=644&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=644&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/745983/original/file-20260705-57-p72fio.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=644&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Stephanie Szarmach holds a yellow-rumped warbler that was banded as part of a study.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Johanna Beam</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Once I spotted a flash of red on one of the bird’s legs, I knew that this individual was special – in fact, it was one that I already knew well. That’s because I had placed <a href="https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds/what-bird-banding">identifying bands</a> on it the previous year as part of my <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-025-00618-6">Ph.D. research</a>, and it was carrying a very important piece of new technology.</p>

<p>I played the <a href="https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Yellow-rumped_Warbler/sounds">high pitched “warble</a>” of its song through a speaker placed below a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aYpH52r3Oz0">mist net</a> of fine, nearly invisible mesh. Thinking another male had intruded on his territory, the bird quickly descended. My tactic worked – he got caught in the net. As I gently removed him, I breathed a sigh of relief as I saw the Tic Tac-size device sitting on his back. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A hand holding a bird that has a small grey device on its back" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755786/original/file-20260824-50-wyl3zv.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A yellow-rumped warbler wears a multisensor geolocator backpack.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Stephanie Szarmach</span></span>
            </figcaption>

<p>Over the past year, this warbler carried a multisensor geolocator backpack throughout his migratory journey, recording the long trek from his breeding grounds in Anchorage, Alaska, to a yet unknown winter refuge and back again. Working with my Ph.D. adviser, evolutionary biologist <a href="https://scholar.google.ca/citations?user=YO4WypkAAAAJ">David Toews</a>, I deployed dozens of these cutting-edge tags to illuminate the migratory journeys of these high-latitude breeding warblers at a scale not previously possible for small birds.</p>

<p>Now, after a year of waiting, I finally had the data in hand. </p>

<h2>How can scientists track small birds?</h2>

<p>Researchers began <a href="https://www.audubon.org/magazine/brief-history-of-how-scientists-have-learned-about-bird-migration">tracking the movements of migrating birds</a> in the late 1960s using <a href="https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds/what-radio-telemetry">radio telemetry</a>, a technique that requires tagged birds to be physically followed with receiver equipment, sometimes aided by a small aircraft.</p>

<p>Then, as GPS became more widely available in the early 2000s, <a href="https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds/what-satellite-telemetry#">satellite tags</a> let researchers accurately track birds remotely. However, GPS transmitters are hefty – even just the battery that powers them is too heavy to be carried by the majority of small migratory songbirds, which often weigh less than a spoonful of sugar.</p>

<p>To address this problem, researchers developed ingenious little <a href="https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds/what-are-light-level-geolocators">light-level geolocators</a>. These miniature tags minimize weight by containing only a tiny battery, clock, computer chip and light sensor. They store data internally rather than transmitting it – hence my need to recapture tagged birds a year later. Researchers infer a bird’s locations from the timing of sunrise and sunset, which vary predictably across the globe and throughout the year.</p>

<p>Light-level geolocators <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1166664">have opened</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2020.1339">new windows into the</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2014.1045">migrations of small birds</a>, but they also have limitations: Their estimated locations can err by hundreds of miles, and this uncertainty becomes impractically high around the equinoxes, when day length is the same worldwide.</p>

In between flights, the pressure the tag records reflects the elevation at the bird’s position.</p>

The unique pattern of rises and falls in pressure acts as a kind of pressure fingerprint for a specific location. Including light and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14082">wind data</a> in the model of the bird’s movements can increase precision even more. </p>

<h2>New tech answers an old question</h2>

<p>We used these new multisensor backpacks to study the migration patterns of <a href="https://www.audubon.org/rockies/news/do-you-know-your-yellow-rumps">myrtle warblers</a>, the northern subspecies of yellow-rumped warbler, which breed across North America’s boreal forest. Myrtle warblers in the northeast are known to winter along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, but where northwestern populations migrate has been more of a mystery. In 1899, ornithologist Richard McGregor <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/1360819">observed myrtle warblers wintering in coastal California</a>, and hypothesized that these birds might breed in Alaska and British Columbia.</p>

<p>Using these new tags allowed us to test whether warblers breeding in Anchorage, Alaska, actually followed the shortest migration route to winter in California. To our surprise – and probably to McGregor’s as well, if he were still alive – we found that all the birds we tracked traveled <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-025-00618-6">east across the boreal forest of Canada before shifting south</a> to the Gulf Coast – certainly not the Pacific Coast route we expected.</p>

<p>All told, this 6,800-mile (10,900-kilometer) round-trip journey was much longer than we anticipated for a species commonly considered a short- or medium-distance migrant.</p>

<h2>Why take such a circuitous route?</h2>

<p>The long, seemingly suboptimal route taken by our Alaskan myrtle warblers is actually mirrored by some other songbird species tracked from northwestern North America, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.2651">blackpoll warblers</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2002.2032">Swainson’s</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2012.1229">thrushes</a>.</p>

<p>Part of this pattern may relate back to the glaciations that isolated ancient populations of birds millions of years ago. The thinking goes that as these glaciers spread, they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2699.2006.01517.x">squashed the ranges</a> of formerly northern species into the south. Then, as the glaciers slowly receded, the forests gradually reexpanded.</p>

<p>As more land opened up, birds moved farther north and west into that habitat. Each season some birds went a little farther as the forest available in their northern breeding grounds expanded. For migratory species such as myrtle warblers, the farther north and west their breeding range expanded, the longer the migration to their southern wintering ground became.</p>

<p>Scientists think migration routes are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2022.07.008">genetically encoded</a>. The birds’ genes may have traced this expansion front, like Hansel and Gretel putting down breadcrumbs as they journeyed deeper and deeper into the forest. Today’s migration routes still trace that incrementally expanded path, even though the glaciers that shaped the original boundaries are long gone.</p>

<p>We’re still not sure exactly where the California-wintering myrtle warblers spotted in the 1800s are breeding. We suspect that a small proportion of the Anchorage-breeding birds <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-025-00618-6">may migrate to California</a>, but that most of them travel from more distant, unstudied regions of Alaska or Yukon. Future research, potentially tagging myrtle warblers directly on the California wintering grounds, will shed more light on this population and why certain individuals follow a different migration route.</p>

<h2>Barometric geolocation provides new data</h2>

<p>Today, this new geolocation approach improves scientists’ ability to study the migrations of small birds and supports more effective conservation actions across the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2015.0552">course of the entire year</a>. More precise location estimates help researchers identify key stopover and wintering sites in need of protection and better understand the threats birds face throughout their journeys. These geolocators also reveal the altitude of migratory flights, which is important for understanding the risk of birds <a href="https://www.audubon.org/landing/protecting-birds-collisions">colliding with buildings</a> or wind turbines.</p>

<p>Because these new tags capture pressure data for every migratory flight, they’re especially valuable for studying migration timing. Researchers have combined data from over 50 bird species to understand at <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.06.030">what time of day or night different birds migrate</a>. Now, as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XIY0uCMAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">postdoctoral researcher</a> at the <a href="https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds">Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center</a>, I am integrating multisensor geolocator data with satellite imagery to investigate how arrival and departure decisions throughout a bird’s migratory journey relate to seasonal changes in plant growth.</p>

<p>Scientists have now tracked dozens of bird species with <a href="https://geopressure.org/GeoLocatorExplorer/">multisensor geolocators</a>, and that number increases every year. Each mapped migratory journey improves our understanding of how small birds migrate, what factors shape their movements and how best to protect them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/284016/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
