title: Trump’s Smithsonian vendetta, briefly explained
excerpt: Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution Lonnie Bunch speaks during an event at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on February 20, 2026, in Was
body: Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution Lonnie Bunch speaks during an event at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on February 20, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: The head of the Smithsonian Institution will resign after weathering nearly two years of attacks by President Donald Trump.  What’s happening? Lonnie G

Bunch III, the secretary of the Smithsonian, announced on Tuesday that he will step down at the end of 2026 after more than seven years in the role.  Bunch’s retirement isn’t entirely about Trump; he’s 73 and has already served longer as secretary than his two most recent predecessors

But the president, who has waged a relentless campaign against what the White House has described as “improper, divisive, or anti-American ideology” at the Smithsonian, is indisputably part of the story

As Bunch put it to the New York Times on Tuesday, “at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.” What has Trump done to the Smithsonian? Since last spring , Trump has gone after the Smithsonian system for promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive.” He has threatened its funding, forced out the director of the National Portrait Gallery, and attempted to meddle with its exhibits
His ability to successfully make changes has been limited by the Smithsonian’s structure — but a new secretary could give Trump far more control

The president also, unsurprisingly, wants more Trump: administration officials have reportedly pressed for a new Portrait Gallery exhibit focusing on the president .  What’s next? Trump doesn’t officially have a role in selecting Bunch’s successor, who will be chosen by the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents — but that board does include Vice President JD Vance and multiple Republican members of Congress, so he might as well

Trump will surely want to install a loyalist, which means — as the Washington Post’s art and architecture critic Philip Kennicott explained on Tuesday — that the Smithsonian’s fate could depend on the ability of the rest of the board, and especially its chancellor, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, to resist

And with that, it’s time to log off… Don’t miss my colleague Rachel Cohen Booth’s new piece on the “smartphone trap” : the way in which phones have become not just ubiquitous, but required for many parts of daily life (reading a menu, parking a car, signing into an account — the list goes on).  As Rachel argues, it’s not too late to preserve, or claw back, the option of going through life phone-free. “Pushing for a non-smartphone option is about accessibility, affordability, and agency
It’s about demanding the kind of freedom in a society we deserve to have,” she writes.  You can read her full story here with a gift link — enjoy, and we’ll see you right back here tomorrow!

body: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand greets members of the audience during a campaign visit to the Cass County Community Center in Cass, Iowa, on August 20, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images Can a love-thy-neighbor, stop-the-division campaign win over masses of rural voters? Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor in Iowa, has his hopes pinned on it.  Key to Sand’s campaign is a promise to end the red-blue warfare in politics

He’s made embracing independents and disgruntled Republicans a core part of his campaign, in addition to ending government corruption, holding big agriculture and big chemical companies responsible for the state’s high cancer rates, and addressing cost-of-living concerns
And his pragmatic approach seems to be working
Polls have reliably shown Sand, who currently serves as Iowa state auditor, ahead of his Republican opponent, Zach Lahn — despite the GOP’s significant voter registration advantage
Democrats haven’t won the governor’s mansion in Iowa since 2006
On top of the gubernatorial race, Iowa also has competitive Senate and House races , which could be key to Democrats’ hopes of gaining control of Congress during this November’s midterm election

To break down what’s happening in Iowa, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Laura Belin, publisher and reporter for the Iowa political website Bleeding Heartland .  Noel and Belin discussed Sand’s unique candidacy, whether it could have lessons for other Democrats looking to succeed in Midwestern states that have grown redder, and how President Donald Trump’s policies could be laying the groundwork for a rural backlash in this year’s midterm elections
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
This midterm season, all eyes seem to be on Iowa
Why is Iowa so crucial? What has happened in Iowa, where we used to be a swing state and we’ve moved into the red column, is not unique to Iowa
Every part of the country that looks like Iowa has seen the same trend of voters moving away from Democrats

It’s happened especially in these working-class communities where the electorate is predominantly white people without a college degree.  Iowa as a whole voted for Barack Obama twice and then voted for Donald Trump three times

So if Democrats can figure out how to start winning again, or at least losing by less, in that kind of area, it could have implications not only for the future of Iowa, but for other states like Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania
What are the main issues that people there are voting on and campaigns are campaigning on? The high cost of everything is definitely the top issue

Democrats have really been hammering on the tariffs and the war in Iran, driving up the cost of everything.  Also, healthcare costs have skyrocketed.  We’ve seen healthcare access be an issue, because we’ve already seen some clinics close, and the companies that control those hospitals or clinics have talked about how it’s partly a reaction to the big Medicaid cuts that were passed in the [GOP’s 2025] budget reconciliation bill
According to many polls that I’ve seen, Trump is underwater in Iowa
His policies are not popular; the tariffs are not popular in Iowa
They’re widely understood to be hurting the Iowa economy
Anyone can see that the cost of everything has gone up
What are the Democrats doing to campaign on that? Are they running on Trump? Most of the Democrats are not running directly against Trump
Rob Sand, the candidate for governor, hardly talks about Donald Trump at all
He really focuses on statewide issues.  Josh Turek, the candidate for Senate, is running [on] the idea that [Republican Senate nominee] Rep
Ashley Hinson has just been a rubber stamp for policies that have hurt Iowa, whether that be the war in Iran [or] tariffs
It’s more running against the Republicans who have been a puppet [for Trump] rather than running against Donald Trump himself
Let’s talk about that governor’s race and Rob Sand
This guy has gotten a fair bit of national interest
What do you know about him? I’ve followed his career for a long time, since he was running for state auditor the first time in 2018
He’s gone out every year, done a hundred town halls a year, done them in every county.  He is reaching out to independents because Iowa Republicans have a pretty large voter registration advantage
So he’s talked a lot about trying to empower independents more in our political spaces
He’s talked about getting Iowa back to divided government
He’s talked about how, with the large Republican majorities we have in the legislature, he would be a check on what they’ve done with 10 years of one-party rule
He used to be a model.  A long time ago, when he was in college
It’s funny, Republicans post these old modeling photos of Rob Sand from the ’90s and even [Sen.] Chuck Grassley’s campaign account posted some of those over the weekend
And I always wonder — I mean, Republicans seem to think that they’re going to get traction out of that, but I don’t really see that as something that Iowans care about at all
I think a more common criticism that I hear is that Rob Sand has a very strong social media presence and has for years

In addition to making videos talking about political issues and what needs to be done in state government, he does a lot of things like reviewing pizza and donuts.  They try to portray him as someone who’s not serious about his job
But I think that that’s just more [that] he has this goofy online persona
And I don’t really think it’s a detriment to his campaign
We’ve seen a certain type of Democrat emerge in the last few years and become very visible this campaign cycle: angry at the Democratic Party, angry at the direction of the country

title: The mystery at the heart of Trump’s trade war
excerpt: Trucks cross into the United States from Canada on the Gordie Howe International Bridge on September 6, 2026. | Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images This story ap
body: Trucks cross into the United States from Canada on the Gordie Howe International Bridge on September 6, 2026. | Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

I spent Labor Day weekend in Montreal, and signs of the trade war were everywhere.  On Google Maps, which — at least until we crossed over the border — jarringly displayed the label “Lake America” where “Lake Ontario” used to be
Along Highway 2, which runs beside the St

Lawrence River, and where lawns sprouted signs with slogans like “Canada, strong and free.” On the TV in the hotel lobby, where a brisk CBC segment reported that Canadians overwhelmingly support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s retaliatory tariffs against the US

Those tariffs, incidentally, went into effect this morning — targeting roughly $20 billion in US products.  The levies are Canada’s response to the 50 percent tariffs that President Donald Trump slapped on Canadian goods in late August, after trade talks between the two countries collapsed
They’ll make it harder for American businesses to sell goods ranging from cheese to golf clubs in Canada, and they’ll make those goods more expensive for Canadians
More worryingly, the new tariffs inflame an ugly dispute that, as I unpack more below, has no apparent upside for the US
President Donald Trump’s aggression toward our northern neighbor has both damaged the country’s international reputation and made life more expensive for average Americans
Go a little deeper View Link Launching a trade war against America’s closest ally is self-evidently…unusual, let’s say
But the strangest thing about Trump’s campaign against Canada is how few people are riding this particular train.  No think tank is churning out anti-Canada papers

No prominent influencer, even, has caught Trump’s eye with dreams of northern conquest.  This sets Canada apart from virtually all of Trump’s other unpopular, fringe positions, which at least have some constituency behind them

Since Trump began musing about Canadian annexation 18 months ago, however, reporters have repeatedly gone out in search of the intellectual and political roots of that fixation…and come back empty-handed.  My colleague Zack Beauchamp made another go of it just last month and concluded, in a word: ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.  Zack talked to a ton of trade experts, political scientists, and Republican strategists and found that — even in industries that have long-standing trade disputes with Canada, and even at think tanks that support economic nationalism more broadly — no one is advocating for the full-scale trade war we’re now experiencing
That vacuum has led many analysts to conclude that Trump’s animus toward Canada is personal, not strategic

And while armchair-psychologizing about this president is risky, his posts about Canada certainly give the impression that he’s after personal and geopolitical domination more than anything else.   On Sunday, Trump posted a cartoon that shows him and Carney dressed as hockey players, with Carney sprawled on the rink in apparent distress

Trump glowers over him: “GET UP, GOVERNOR,” a speech bubble says.  It might be the most insight we get into the real motivations for a trade war that’s steadily intensifying, with no resolution in sight.  One link for later ➨ Ditch the plastic food packaging
A new peer-reviewed study concluded that it’s impossible to evaluate the safety of most chemicals used in food processing and packaging — companies just don’t make enough data public for that
So in the absence of regulation that mandates more disclosure, you’re probably better off storing your food in an eclectic collection of tiny jars

Before you go… Did you know… that rats probably don’t deserve all the blame for the Black Death ? Researchers are investigating a surprising and gross range of potential plague-carriers, including sheep, lice, fleas, and camels.  Today’s trivia: Skye is the largest island in what archipelago? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the world’s second-largest living bird
That would be the emu , which can reach 130 pounds and run at speeds of up to 31 miles per hour.

title: How Christians can fight back against Christian nationalism
excerpt: Community faith leaders gather for a prayer vigil on the second anniversary of January 6 in 2023 in Washington, DC
body: Community faith leaders gather for a prayer vigil on the second anniversary of January 6 in 2023 in Washington, DC

Speakers called for an end to Christian nationalism and denounced political violence. | Nathan Howard/Getty Images Are we on the precipice of a white Christian nationalist takeover?  The author and religion scholar Robert P
Jones sure feels like we’re close. “This is our 1933,” he writes in his new book, referencing the year that Weimar Germany fell to a Nazi takeover
Panicked allusions to Nazi Germany have been a common occurrence in the Trump years

But Jones, who has studied religion for decades and grew up Southern Baptist, has a very specific perspective on why those references are warranted now, particularly because of the role Christians played then — and it all worries him
It was in 1933, Jones writes, that the German Lutheran pastor Martin Niemöller began resisting Nazi rule
He was arrested four years later and imprisoned at the Dachau concentration camp until 1945

Revisiting Dachau after World War II, Niemöller remembered 1933 as not just the year the camp opened, nor a reminder of a time when he was still a free man, but also a marker of how much time he had wasted in the preceding years supporting the Nazis
From their rise in the 1920s until that moment, he’d been supportive of much of the Nazis’ movement, voting for them in three different elections
After his release, every day of that time felt like a missed opportunity to do something to avert a tragedy
Jones doesn’t make this historical parallel lightly

In his new book, Backslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracy , he spends a significant amount of time building the case that the actions of the second Trump administration, combined with rock-solid support from white Christian evangelicals , are resulting in escalating religious authoritarianism, pointing to evangelical support for mass deportations earlier this year and Christian nationalist rhetoric by members of the administration, such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “We are now living in a democratically back-slidden nation, abetted by an apostate white Christianity,” he writes
But his book isn’t just a panicked observation; it’s a call to action
Like Niemöller, he argues, religious people who’ve sat out or passively supported MAGA can still effect change
And churches are just as important to stopping a slide into religiously backed authoritarianism as many were in abetting its rise

So what should Christians who don’t buy into this vision of their faith do to resist it?  Jones is the president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute , the leading research and polling think tank on politics and religion, and a scholar of religion — spending his career analyzing and writing books on the relationship between race, white supremacy, and faith in America
I decided to chat with him to figure out what the road map for Christian resistance to Christian nationalism might look like
Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity

Why are you taking on this project now? If you look back at the three previous books I’ve written in the last decade, they have been responding in various ways to the rise of Christian nationalism that we’ve seen in the country and the threat that that poses
This book is motivated by a sense of urgency

I’m also trying to turn the corner in this book by saying, For those of us who care about the integrity of Christianity and the future of democracy, the real question is what are we going to do in this moment ? Throughout the book, you argue that there is very little daylight between what the administration is doing and what white Christian evangelicals will support
I think immigration policy comes to mind: that it’s hard to propose draconian enforcement policies that these Christians won’t tolerate

Do you really expect people to change? So the line you’re thinking about — because I remember writing this line — it was, “In the Trump era, white evangelical attitudes about undocumented immigrants are so extreme that it seems virtually impossible to construct a policy that is too brutal for them to support.” I go through the options [offered in PRRI polling ]: Do you support putting things like razor wire and barricades in a river that might make people drown? Yep, we’re good with that
Do you put people in internment camps? Yep, we’re good with that

And so I do think it should be shocking to hear those kinds of responses, again, from people who say they follow a Bible that talks more about caring for the widow or the orphan and has a lot to say about immigrants and the stranger who resides among you and being kind to them, not oppressing them
I even say at the beginning of the book, I’m not writing for the people who have completely given themselves over to this MAGA worldview
And the evidence shows that it is the vast majority of white evangelicals that have done that
But among white Catholics, among white mainline Protestants, it’s less of a complete acquiescence to that seductive political worldview

That’s who I’m writing to.  “The biggest challenge has been apathy among many white Christians who have watched this extremism take hold, have watched it grow, and have really been uncomfortable speaking out.” I’m a pragmatist on this point

At the end of the book, I talk about the need for division, and that we have to realize that there are going to be some people who are so wedded to this kind of power and violence that they’re beyond persuasion
The only solution is to out-organize and resist that movement and to stand up something else in its wake.  We’re starting to see some of that as well
White evangelicals only make up 13 percent of the country
And even though almost 85 percent of them are all in on the MAGA movement, that’s nowhere near a majority of the country
And even if you take everyone who supports a Christian nationalist worldview, it’s only about three in 10 Americans
Now that’s a lot, and it’s a majority of Republicans and it’s two-thirds of white evangelicals in that camp

But it does mean that the country as a whole rejects that worldview by a margin of 2-to-1.  The biggest challenge has been apathy among many white Christians who have watched this extremism take hold, have watched it grow, and have really been uncomfortable speaking out and saying, Wait, wait, wait, that’s not how I understand Christianity
That’s not how I understand the Bible or the teachings of Jesus
And so I think this book is in some ways aimed at that group and saying, Yeah, it’s kind of now or never
If you want a different version of Christianity to exist in this country, it’s time to stand one up and make it a very publicly visible thing

So where does that leave us in terms of resisting and out-organizing? What is the playbook for beating back this takeover? I’m pretty convinced that if we’re talking about persuading the folks that have been all in for Trump for a decade now, for three consecutive elections, that’s a fool’s errand

title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
excerpt: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brough
body: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week
The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period
In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas
A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people
Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region
More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas
At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes
On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing

How much hydrogen awaits us underground? A flurry of exploration efforts is searching for underground stores of hydrogen gas, which could provide a valuable source of zero-carbon fuel

The hunt has spread all over the world and engaged dozens of startups, including the Bill Gates–backed Koloma, which has been poking around the US Midwest to reach ancient oceanic rocks associated with hydrogen production
But the search so far has come up short.  No one has yet reported finding a commercially viable reservoir of the gas, and public data on what has been found remains in short supply
Yet researchers estimate that trillions of tons of H₂ are produced within Earth’s crust
If a small fraction could be recovered, it could meet global hydrogen demand for centuries

title: Your food may be safe. Its packaging is another story.
excerpt: Baby food pouches, in particular, carry a higher chemical exposure risk. | Jeffrey Greenberg, Universal Images Group via Getty Images This story was originally
body: Baby food pouches, in particular, carry a higher chemical exposure risk. | Jeffrey Greenberg, Universal Images Group via Getty Images This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration
Most people decide if it’s safe to eat an old tub of yogurt in the fridge or canned tuna in the back of the cupboard by checking its sell-by date
But no label indicates that pesticides, phthalates, PFAS, or other hazardous chemicals could be seeping from those containers into your food
Of more than 15,000 chemicals that come in contact with food, a new  peer-reviewed study  found that 1,222 pose serious health risks such as cancer and reproductive harm
And the vast majority — 87 percent, or more than 13,200 — lack enough accessible information to even estimate their risks

The fact that there’s not enough publicly available information for independent scientists to assess the safety of chemicals that can contaminate food is “the elephant in the room,” said study co-author Jane Muncke, managing director at the nonprofit Food Packaging Forum Foundation, which led the research, published Tuesday in the journal Environmental Science & Technology .  Consumers trust that when regulators allow chemicals in products like food packaging, it’s because it’s been through safety testing, Muncke said. “But that’s not the case,” she said. “And it doesn’t make sense.” The team has done a “very, very good job” highlighting how little is known about the risks of substances that affect everyone, said Maricel Maffini, an independent chemical safety and regulation expert who was not involved in the study but has collaborated with Muncke in the past.  Because the study focused on a list that people in industry and regulators regard as reliable, it’s looking under the proverbial lamppost, Maffini said

While there’s plenty of information suggesting that many of these chemicals should not be on the market or should have stronger regulations, she said, there’s so much information beyond that list that’s missing

In previous work, Muncke and her team identified more than 15,000 chemicals used in food processing or packaging from lists of substances approved by regulators in the United States, China, Japan, and countries in Europe and South America or that had been  identified in studies

In the new paper, they analyzed that “jaw-dropping” number of chemicals, Muncke said, to flag the most problematic.  To maximize the utility of their priority list, the team used only data obtained from governmental and regulatory agencies linking a chemical to human health hazards such as cancer, reproductive harm, or ability to concentrate in the body
That yielded a priority list of 1,222 chemicals that they ranked into four tiers, with the highest to lowest evidence of human exposure from food-contact materials

Ninety-four chemicals known to seep into food and detected in breast milk, blood, or other  human samples  were assigned to Tier 1, the highest priority for regulators and companies to consider phasing out

These chemicals include liver- and immune system-damaging PFAS “forever chemicals,” which make food wrappers grease- or water-resistant; the likely carcinogen  styrene , used to produce takeout packages and  refrigerated dairy food  containers; hormone-disrupting  phthalates , added to make plastics like those that hold  vegetable oils  flexible; and bisphenol A, added to hard plastics and can linings and a  poster child  for endocrine disruptors’ ability to impair development at low doses

Studies have found these and other chemicals leaching from containers into a diverse array of food and beverages, including  water, infant formula ,  orange juice ,  ice cream ,  yogurt and cream ,  oils, cake, and fatty foods
The next highest priority list, Tier 2, included an additional 264 hazardous chemicals that  leach into food  but have not been detected in biomonitoring studies

Recommendations to protect consumers Experts with the Food Packaging Forum say regulators can take simple steps to reduce people’s exposure to harmful chemicals found or used in food-contact materials, starting with moving away from evaluating one chemical at a time
People are exposed to multiple synthetic chemicals simultaneously through food-contact materials, textiles, personal-care products, air pollution, and more
Regulators should introduce a “mixture allocation factor,” which creates a safety margin that accounts for the combined effects of multiple chemicals in a single exposure

If there is sufficient evidence that individual chemicals in a group with similar structures and properties are hazardous, then all members of that group should be pulled from the market or not approved until proven safe, as the European Union did in its 2023 proposal to restrict PFAS as a group

Modify rules for material safety to ensure that what escapes from products is safe under different use conditions and expand screening of toxicity to include chronic disease outcomes like diabetes, infertility, and harm to the immune and nervous systems
Determine if chemicals or materials like glass or stainless steel classified as inert leach into food
If they don’t leach, they’re not a priority for in-depth chemical analysis
Inert materials that can be reused should be the policy goal
The chemicals in Tier 1 provide the most reliable evidence that materials that come in contact with food are a source of people’s exposure to these chemicals, Muncke said

The chemicals are in people, they’re in food, and they’re in food-contact materials, she said. “What more proof do you want?” Inside Climate News asked the American Chemistry Council and Food Packaging Coalition, trade groups that represent the chemical and food-packing industries, if their members would release hazard information about the chemicals they use and phase out those known to be hazardous

Neither responded, but the Food Packaging Coalition maintains that packaging is designed to prevent the transfer of its components to food and to ensure that they are safe and suitable for their intended use.  The paper offers a practical and transparent roadmap for using the best available evidence to prioritize food-contact chemicals for regulation, said Sara Lupolt, an expert on exposure assessment at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who was not involved in the research.  Though not addressed in the paper, she added, more research is needed to determine which foods and chemical combinations result in more chemicals moving into food
Plastic chemicals in baby food Many of the chemicals that migrate into food are so-called non-intentionally added substances, (NIAS)

Their identity is often obscure because existing tools can’t identify every chemical in use, especially when researchers don’t know what to look for because producers keep proprietary chemical ingredients secret
Muncke is particularly concerned about babies’ exposure to plastic chemicals in pouches that hold juices and pureed food
Earlier this year, her team found evidence that more than 330 chemicals leach from pouches, including nearly 80 known to be hazardous
They presented the findings at  an event  at the House of Lords in the United Kingdom in June
A greater volume of chemicals gets into baby food because the ratio of packaging to food is much greater in a small serving size, Muncke said

And the pouches are sterilized using heat, which drives chemicals to migrate and forms microplastics.  Several  peer-reviewed  studies, including a  2023 Chemosphere study , also found chemicals, including NIAS, in baby food packaged in pouches

The paper’s authors believed the NIAS, which lacked adequate information to assess risk, were impurities and raw materials from producing plastic. “Infants may be constantly exposed to NIAS via consuming pouched food products,” the authors warned

For the 87 percent of chemicals that lack hazard data, it’s primarily a question of the data not being public, said study co-author Helene Wiesinger, a chemist and Food Packaging Forum scientific officer.  That delays regulatory action, Wiesinger said, because governments and independent scientists must first figure out which chemicals are safe
She believes a product or chemical should not be allowed on the market until a company can prove that it’s safe
At a minimum, chemicals that have structural similarities with others known to be hazardous should be priorities for regulation, the paper argues

Seventy percent of the more than 4,200 chemicals the team classified into 38 priority groups — including PFAS, phthalates and organophosphates (used as flame retardants and pesticides, among other applications) — lack enough data to assess potential harms
Just because something isn’t yet known to be hazardous doesn’t mean it’s not hazardous, Wiesinger said

Time and again, chemicals found to present unreasonable risks are replaced with others that have similar properties and ultimately similar risks. “We hope this work provides practical guidance on how to at least not make the very obvious mistakes,” she said.

title: Data centers are bringing Americans together
excerpt: Protesters rally against data centers at the Texas State Capitol in Austin, Texas, on July 27, 2026. | Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images
body: Protesters rally against data centers at the Texas State Capitol in Austin, Texas, on July 27, 2026. | Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images The data center backlash has entered the midterms conversation.  Politicians from across the spectrum have changed their minds — or at least their policy positions — about data centers in the past few months as public resistance to their construction has skyrocketed
A major example is Texas, where just about one year ago, Republican Gov

Greg Abbott was proclaiming that his state was the “epicenter of AI development.” Now, after months of grassroots organizing and community outcry, Abbott is pushing to slow the roll of new data centers in Texas
He’s imposed a statewide moratorium on new construction pending an audit over the new connections to Texas’s power grid
While he hasn’t explicitly said the change is tied to his reelection campaign this November, the pause is expected to last through the election
As dramatic as Abbott’s about-face has been, he’s not alone: Democrats and Republicans alike are following suit

Jeremy Merrill , a data reporter at the Washington Post, analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see what elected officials on both sides of the aisle are saying about data centers

He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about his findings, what they say going into midterm elections, and how the backlash might change the way we think about what politicians owe to their constituents
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  What did you find? Data centers didn’t used to be a big deal
And now, almost all of a sudden, they’re a big issue
Candidates are falling over themselves to sound tough about data centers
And data centers are overwhelmingly portrayed as a problem rather than an opportunity or a benefit.  A great example is Sen
Jon Husted, who’s a Republican senator from Ohio, who’s up for election this November

He used to praise data center projects that were coming to Ohio when he was lieutenant governor because it would help establish Ohio as “an important tech hub in America.” He said that data centers are essential to our digital lives

And now he’s saying he’s trying to “protect Americans from having to foot the bill for data centers.” He’s really emblematic of a shift that happened all across the Republican Party in about February of this year

That’s when the bulk of messages from Republicans about data centers flipped from focusing on them as bringing benefits to their states and communities, to talking about their downsides.  This is really a case of the anger and unhappiness bubbling up from everyday people up to political elites

And that grassroots anger was all across the political spectrum over a whole range of issues: power bills, claims about how much water data centers may use, air pollution, eminent domain, taxes, subsidies, and a generalized, physical manifestation of the anxiety that people feel about what AI is going to do to our society, to our brains, to our kids and to our jobs

We know that it’s not just one single candidate, maybe even not just a handful, because you reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that, “Data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”  That’s pretty strong language

Is the National Republican Senatorial Committee admitting that the wrong position on data centers is enough to lose a candidate a race at this point? I think it’s something that they’re certainly worried about

And presumably you’re looking for an edge, or to prevent your opponent from getting an edge over you.  What about President Donald Trump’s messaging on data centers? He, initially at least, was very bullish on AI investment in the US
What has Trump been saying? This is a story in two or three parts

As President Trump took office again last year, he was overall trying to portray his second term as president as “inaugurating a golden age for American manufacturing and technological dominance.” As part of that, he issued an executive order trying to make it easier to build data centers in the United States

And I think that’s probably why last year most Republicans across the board were talking about data centers as a benefit to the country and to the communities where they were being built — talking about jobs, talking about investment
And so on the one hand, you have President Trump promoting this bill that would protect people from having data centers cause their power bills to go up

But on the other hand, he just wrote earlier this week on Truth Social, “If [communities] want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” He’s saying if they don’t want data centers, they’re going to “end up being backwards and poor.” So he’s still very pro-data center, which is fascinating
Which Democrats in particular are we seeing change their minds? There are a lot of governors who used to be very positive on data centers in their states because these bring jobs
These bring construction investments, some amount of permanent jobs, some amount of construction jobs
Examples of folks who are now limiting data centers in their states include Gov
Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and [Gov.] J.B
The most striking case of a Democrat whose rhetoric has shifted so much is Rep
Ro Khanna of California, whose district actually includes Silicon Valley
In 2025, he was calling for building more data centers in the United States versus overseas

When the Trump administration did an AI deal with the United Arab Emirates, he said, “Why are we putting data centers and research hubs in Dubai?”  But now he’s more critical, calling for an end to data center extraction, taking communities’ water and jacking up their bills, sucking all the money into the hands of a few tech billionaires
Is anyone in either party still coming out strong for data centers? My favorite example of this is Rep
Eric Burlison, who’s a Republican from Missouri
He’s really focused on the need to build data centers in order to compete with China

In June, he wrote, “Ask yourself who benefits when Americans turn against data centers? China does.” He’s making the point that I think a lot of people in tech are making, which is, “This is coming whether you like it or not.” And part of politics is dealing with reality

In this day and age, it seems constituents don’t want to deal with that reality, but clearly there are people who hold office, or who hope to hold office, who are going to maintain the line that this is something we’ve just got to do
This is a classic political science dispute about what a politician’s job is supposed to be
